activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
story:
Ashton arrived at the theater eleven minutes early, which was a mistake, because it left him standing under the marquee with nothing to do but rehearse the opening line he'd already abandoned twice on the walk over. Daniela was never early. Daniela operated on a theory, he suspected, that being on time was a kind of surrender. He'd liked that about her since sophomore year, along with roughly nine other things he'd never said out loud.

When she came around the corner in her green jacket, he waved and immediately regretted the wave, which was too big, the wave of a man flagging a taxi. She waved back anyway, smaller, and said, "You bought tickets already, didn't you."

"Statistically, yes."

Inside, the lobby smelled like melted butter and carpet shampoo, that specific theater smell that hadn't changed since he was seven. He paid for the popcorn, she paid for the drinks, and they found seats in the middle of the row, third from the back, which she declared the only correct row, and he agreed, because he had read that agreeing with someone early made everything after easier. He'd spent the last three nights reading about things like that.

Two weeks earlier, Mr. Pierre had passed around a psych article in the elective Ashton took mostly to fill his schedule. In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh had found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. Nicolas, reading over Ashton's shoulder, had said, "So just copy whatever she does and she's yours," and Mr. Pierre had said something about how the study wasn't a pickup manual, it was about how much of the mind runs below the surface, which had only made Nicolas grin harder. Ashton had rolled his eyes at the time. He had also copied the sentence into his phone.

The trailers started. Ashton ate a piece of popcorn, waited a reasonable interval, and noticed Daniela settle her elbow on the armrest, chin in her palm. He let a minute pass, then set his own elbow on the other armrest, chin in his own palm, a move he attempted to disguise as getting comfortable. She didn't glance over. Good, he thought. Not noticing was the whole point; that was what the study had found, that it worked even without the person noticing. He felt like a spy, and also like an idiot, and the two feelings sat together in his chest without resolving.

Twenty minutes into the movie, a dragon did something impressive, and Daniela leaned forward, and Ashton leaned forward, and then she leaned back and so did he, and by the third occasion he had to admit a problem: he couldn't tell whether he was doing the mimicking or whether she was. She'd propped her feet on the seat in front of her before he had. She'd started nodding at the hero's speeches slightly before he did. It was possible she'd read the same article. It was possible neither of them was doing anything and two people in the same dark room just move like people. The veracity of his own experiment was now beyond reach, and he'd designed it himself.

He tested her once, deliberately. He dropped his hand flat on the armrest between them, palm up, the least natural posture available to a human body. Ninety seconds. Nothing. He closed his hand and put it back in his lap, and Daniela, without turning from the screen, said, "That was the worst thing I've ever watched a person do with their hand."

"I was stretching."

"You were doing science." She pulled her feet down and turned to look at him, finally, her face lit blue by the explosion happening behind them. "Nicolas told me you saved that mimicry thing Mr. Pierre gave us. Tanya Chartrand, John Bargh, 1999. He thought it was hilarious. I thought it was hilarious. Then I thought about it in the shower for like ten minutes."

The movie's hero was shouting something ebullient about destiny while they both faced the screen again, side by side, neither of them sure whose posture belonged to whom anymore. The trailers had valorized honesty, he remembered, in that breathless way trailers have, and honesty seemed suddenly both obvious and impossible. "So did it work?" he asked. "The article. Did I like you more?"

"That's the thing," Daniela said. "There's no control group." She reached over and took a piece of his popcorn, and then, a moment later, he reached over and took a piece of hers.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
Anais had been given the keys to the gym, or rather the clipboard, which in Mr. Ostrowski's absence amounted to the same thing. The grade eight feeder team was hers for three practices, and their passes kept dying on the tape of nothing at all, because a defender's stick, patient as a toll booth, sat in the lane every single time. She'd watched two periods of it from the bench, chewing her pen, and by the end she had a whole page of evidence and no verdict.

"They can't pass through sticks," she told Milena in the changerooom hallway, holding the pen like a gavel. "So either we teach them to pass around sticks, or we teach them sticks don't matter."

"Those are two very sectarian positions," Milena said, draping herself over the water fountain. "Like the reformed church of cycling the puck versus the old believers of just shooting it." Milena knew almost nothing about hockey, which Anais had decided made her an excellent sounding board, since she never argued from experience.

The truth was Anais had two voices in her head, and they disagreed. Her own coach had always drilled passing around pressure: wheel, regroup, find the open lane. But her neighbour, the one who watched junior games on a lawn chair in his garage, had spent one entire October evening insisting that good teams passed over trouble, not around it, lifting the puck so it sailed clean and came down flat on the receiver's blade. She'd filed it away as the rambling of a man who called icing "the cold thing." Now it surfaced like a log she'd forgotten she'd stacked.

At the second practice she ran both. The around-drill first, cones and options, which the kids executed with the joy of people filing taxes. Then she dragged a blue pad to the blue line and made it the toll booth, and told them to get the puck past it. First attempts were disasters, flip shots that helicoptered end over end and landed in Leanne's skates, once in Leanne's helmet. "I've been amortized," Leanne announced from the ice, meaning she had taken the cost of everyone's bad technique all at once, and even the kids laughed, which was the first laugh of the week.

Then Anais remembered the garage man's exact words, or close enough, and stood on the faceoff dot. "You want a saucer pass," she said. "Lift it just off the ice, so it flies flat over the stick and lands on the blade." She demonstrated, badly, the puck wobbling like a thrown frisbee, but the idea landed even where her puck didn't. The kids lined up and tried again, and the syntax of it started to make sense to her as she watched: the roll of the wrists at release, the small arc, the receiver standing still with his blade flat like a plate waiting for dinner.

The third practice, the scrimmages changed. Pucks began hopping over defenders' sticks and settling, some of them, onto waiting blades. Not all. Maybe a third of them still climbed too high or knuckled sideways, and Anais wrote that down too, because she didn't want to pretend the problem was solved when it was only introduced. Her two voices had stopped arguing, mostly. Around when you can, over when you must, and the tricky part, the part she'd underlined twice, was knowing which was which, and she suspected nobody fully knew, they just decided faster.

The twist arrived at the end of practice, in the person of Padma, the smallest kid on the team, who had spent three days at the end of the bench appearing to do nothing. Ms. Bui, the teacher supervising the gym, pointed her out. "That one's been landing those flat little passes all season," she said. "We assumed she was just lucky." Anais watched Padma saucer a puck over a defender's stick, an easy, modest arc, flat as a table, onto a teammate's tape, and then look over at the clipboard as if to ask whether that was allowed.

Anais skated over, held out the pen, and said, "Okay. You take the next drill."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Brown nitrogen dioxide forms colourless dinitrogen tetroxide in an exothermic reaction, so a sealed tube of the gas turns paler when cooled and darker brown when warmed.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and old paint, and Mr. Pelletier had cleared one end of the workbench just for them, sweeping the shavings into his palm like a man clearing a table before a meal he wasn't sure anyone would stay for. Justine set down the cooler of ice, the kettle she'd borrowed from her mother, and her notebook, open to a page with the unit test date circled twice. She needed this. She had failed the last quiz on equilibrium so badly that Mr. Pelletier, who lived three houses down and had once taught chemistry at the high school, had stopped her on the sidewalk and said, "You're thinking of it as a recipe. It's more like a negotiation."

Shawn arrived with Aydan, carrying a thermos and the sealed glass tube Mr. Pelletier had lent them, wrapped in a dish towel. The gas inside was brown, the brown of strong tea, of river water in August. Justine had read the textbook section four times and understood none of it, which was its own kind of humiliation, because she understood most things on the second read.

"Okay," she said. "Ice first." She filled a beaker from the cooler and lowered the tube into it, holding it by the top with the tongs because the video she'd watched said not to touch the glass. Shawn leaned in. Aydan leaned in. For a moment nothing happened, and Justine felt the familiar panic that she'd done it wrong, that she'd misunderstood even this.

Then the brown began to fade. It paled from the bottom up, like dusk running backward, until the tube held something only faintly tinted, nearly colourless, and Aydan said, "Whoa," in the hushed voice people used for things that weren't tricks but felt like them.

"Two molecules of the brown one," Justine said slowly, reading her own notes and watching the tube at the same time. "Nitrogen dioxide. They join up into dinitrogen tetroxide, and that one's colourless. So when it's cold, there's more of the colourless kind." She paused. "And the joining is exothermic. It gives off heat. That part I actually remember."

She lifted the tube out and sat it on the bench, and Shawn poured hot water from the thermos into a second beaker while Aydan texted someone, thumb moving fast, face turned slightly away. Justine noticed the turn but let it go; she was busy, and being busy was, she had learned, a reliable place to hide from the question of why Aydan had stopped sitting with her at lunch. She lowered the tube into the warm water, and the brown came back like a stain spreading through cloth, deeper than before, rich and dark, and she wrote pale when cold, dark when warm and underlined it twice.

"So cooling pushes it one way and warming pushes it the other," she said. "The gas isn't deciding anything. It's just that the balance shifts." She looked at the two beakers side by side, the tube in the dark one like a held breath. "That's the principle. You disturb it, it shifts to counteract the disturbance." She glanced at Mr. Pelletier, who was arranging jars on a shelf and pretending not to listen, which was how he supervised, and she suspected he'd known that about himself for decades.

"It's like us," Shawn said, and Justine waited for him to introspect, to say something about people shifting when pressured, but he only shrugged and said, "Never mind, that's cheesy," and drank his tea. Later, when Aydan had gone home early with a mumbled excuse, Justine helped Mr. Pelletier carry boxes to the curb, boxes labelled KITCHEN and BOOKS, and understood without being told that the house was being emptied, that the garage she'd learned in would belong to strangers by summer. She stood in the doorway holding the tube of pale brown gas, one end still warm from her hand, and watched him tape the last box shut.

She knew the colour would darken again in her closed fist and pale in the evening air, back and forth, back and forth, never settling. "Can I keep it till the test?" she asked, and Mr. Pelletier looked at the tube, then at her, and handed her the dish towel to wrap it in.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down.
story:
I understood monetary policy perfectly, which was why I was lying on the kitchen floor at nine on a Saturday morning with a textbook open to a diagram I had already read four times. Ms. Halvorsen had announced on Thursday that our economics class would run a question period on Monday, and that each of us had to be ready to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She said it as though it were obvious. It was not obvious to me, and I had decided the fault lay with the textbook.

The house was quiet except for the dishwasher. My mother had gone to the market, my father to his workshop, and I had the kitchen table to myself: notes, highlighters, a mug of tea going cold. I understood it perfectly. That was my position and I was holding to it. Whenever a sentence in the textbook defeated me, I underlined it, which is a form of winning.

Melina arrived around ten with Farhan, because I had texted them both that I was hopeless, though I phrased it as "study session, my place, I basically have this down." Farhan brought the good cookies. Melina brought her little brother's lemonade stand cashbox, because she had a theory that economics only made sense if you acted it out, a theory she had developed the previous semester to pass chemistry and now applied to everything, including an argument about bus fares.

"Right," she said, setting the cashbox on the table. "We're a lemonade stand. Our costs go up, everyone's costs go up. Do we raise our price now or later?"

"Later," Farhan said. "You don't raise before you have to."

"No, now," Melina said. "Because next month the cups cost more, and the month after that more again, so if we wait we're always behind. You have to get ahead of it."

"You're describing expectations," I said, and I said it with such authority that I surprised myself, because I had not known I knew it until it left my mouth. I had a fleeting reverie of Ms. Halvorsen nodding at me on Monday, and I stayed in it a moment too long, because Farhan was watching me.

"Go on," he said.

I looked at my underlined sentence. When I finally let myself read it honestly, instead of merely conquering it with a highlighter, it said something specific: if people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down. I had been treating this as decoration around the real mechanism, whatever the real mechanism was. It occurred to me, slowly, the way a smell reaches you from another room, that this might be the mechanism.

"Okay," I said. "The stand. You want to raise the price because you expect everything else to cost more next month."

"Obviously," said Melina.

"But what if you trusted someone to keep prices from going up. Not the lemonade, everything. If you actually believed it."

Melina frowned at her cashbox. "Then I wouldn't be in a hurry. I'd ask for a smaller raise. Ask for less, wait it out."

"Exactly. And if everybody asks for smaller wage and price increases, then inflation stays down. The expectation does part of the work. It's ductile, sort of. It bends depending on what people believe." I was reaching and I knew it, but the sentence held. "So when the central bank raises rates, it's not only the rates doing the slowing. People watch it happen, and if they trust the bank, they expect less inflation, and they behave accordingly, and the expectation itself helps keep inflation down."

Farhan ate a cookie in a way that suggested deliberation. "So the bank is spending its credibility," he said. "Every time it does what it said it would."

"That's a nicer sentence than any in this book," I said, and I meant it, and I also noted the part I had not said aloud: I still did not understand why raising rates slowed anything in the first place, apart from the expectation part, and I was not going to pretend otherwise on Monday. Ms. Halvorsen could ask her follow-up question and find the hole. At least now I would know where it was.

Melina snapped the cashbox shut. "So we keep the price at fifty cents," she said, "on the understanding that somebody out there is in charge."

"Nobody's in charge of lemonade," Farhan said.

"Somebody's in charge of something," Melina said, and opened the cashbox again, and began counting out coins for cups that would cost exactly what they cost today.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: APY, annual percentage yield, includes the effect of compounding, so a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY.
story:
The credit union had set up a folding table outside the cafeteria on the last Tuesday of August, and Samantha stopped at it because she had forty minutes to kill and twelve dollars in her checking account. Behind the table a woman in a navy vest was taping up a poster that read, in letters sized for a highway, 4.75% APY. Beside the poster, a stack of brochures, and on the brochure's back page, in gray type small enough to feel like a dare, a different number: 4.65% compounded monthly. Samantha read it twice, then a third time, because the two figures were printed for the same account, and she was eighteen and had until Friday to decide whether to sign the loan papers on a six-year-old Civic.

The loan was the whole problem. The Civic cost 4,300 dollars, her summer job at the garden center had produced 1,900 of it, and her father, who could be belligerent about money the way other people's fathers were about lawn care, had offered to co-sign. The dealer's financing sheet said 11.2 percent, a number Samantha had stared at for a long time before noticing a second number, smaller, further down, that told her how much she would actually pay over three years. It was more. It was more in a way that felt like a rule she should have been taught.

"They're both real," said Adrienne, who had drifted over from the vending machines with a bag of chips. She tapped the poster and then the brochure. "Four sixty-five and four seventy-five. Same account."

"So one of them is lying."

"Or it's like taxes. Advertised price versus actual price."

Adrienne wanted the table's free pen. She wanted it the way she wanted most free things, which was completely and without apology, and she had already palmed one while they talked. Samantha took the brochure instead and sat down on the wide concrete lip of the planter, where the noon sun had baked the gravel pale, and the courtyard opened around her like a small steppe of backpacks and skateboards and one lost mitten nobody had claimed since June.

Elle found her there fifteen minutes later, sat down, and read the brochure upside down first, then right side up. "My mom's a teller," she said. "She says people yell about this every week." Elle pulled out her phone, typed for a while, and turned the screen around. A bank page, an FAQ, and a definition sitting there in plain sight. "It's called APY," she read. "Annual percentage yield." The page said that APY includes the effect of compounding, so that a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY. Samantha read it aloud, slowly, the way she'd learned to read lab instructions, and felt something settle, the two numbers stopping their argument and agreeing to be the same number wearing different clothes.

"Okay," she said. "So the bigger one isn't a lie, and it isn't a bonus. It's the small one with the months counted in." Which meant the account would actually earn a hair more than the rate alone suggested, that interest could sit on interest and the bank had a word for it. She thought of the dealer's sheet, the 11.2 percent and the smaller number underneath that was somehow the bigger amount. The rule ran in both directions, then. It grew what you kept and it grew what you owed, and nobody put that on a poster in highway letters.

She wanted to be sure she wasn't fooling herself, so after last period she went to the library, where Ms. Bighorn was wheeling a cart of returned geography textbooks toward the far shelves. Samantha asked whether the library had anything on interest, expecting to be handed a lecture. Ms. Bighorn squinted at her, pulled a thin book called Personal Finance for Beginners off a shelf the Dewey system had delimited with brutal precision, and said only, "Chapter four. Don't write in it." She went back to the cart. Samantha took the book to the window table and read chapter four twice, checking the brochure numbers against a table in the book, running her finger down the columns, and the numbers matched, and nowhere did the book tell her whether six years of a Civic was worth it.

That part stayed open, honestly. Saving the full amount meant another year of bus rides and borrowed rides and her father's face at the mention of the bus. Borrowing meant the compounding ran the other way, quietly, in the dark of monthly statements. She copied the APY line into her notebook, then the loan figures, and set her pen down between them like a fence that fenced nothing.

Outside, Adrienne was still in the parking lot, clicking the free pen at the sky. Samantha folded the brochure into her back pocket and walked out to her. "Sign it or not?" Adrienne asked. Samantha clicked the pen once herself before handing it back. "Ask me Friday," she said.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
The bus smelled of rain and wet canvas, and Jade sat with her knees against the seat ahead, holding her phone so the screen wouldn't show. On it was a draft message she'd started four times: Kayson, about the debate slides. He'd promised them Tuesday night and delivered them at six in the morning, half-built, and their round was tomorrow. She'd typed "you ruined it" first. Then deleted it. Then typed it again, gentler, and deleted that too.

Katherine dropped into the seat beside her, shaking water off her sleeves. "You look like you're drafting a eulogy."

"Feedback for Kayson. About the slides."

"The turbid ones with the clip art eagles?" Katherine had a way of making Jade's problems sound like shared jokes, which was partly why Jade told her things. "You could just tell him they were late."

"I did, kind of. He got quiet and said sorry twice, and then I felt like a bully, so I said it was fine, which it isn't." Jade looked out at the flooded field going past. "Mr. Tang had this thing on the board last week. I only half read it."

Katherine pulled out her own notes, flipped pages of her handwriting, and turned the notebook around. At the top, underlined twice: I-messages. "'I felt stuck when the slides came in late.' Thomas Gordon, the psychologist. He promoted them in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming." She tapped the page. "He made us practise turning 'you ruined it' into one. You were out getting the tripod."

"So it's not some trick with the word I."

"It's just what happened to you, said plain. You don't get to say what he did wrong, exactly. You say what it did to you." Katherine shrugged. "Kayson's not a mind reader, and he's not fragile either. He's just embarrassed."

Jade had a presentiment that the conversation would still go wrong somehow, that she'd open her mouth and the old habit would come out, the one where kindness meant saying nothing at all. But she took the notebook anyway and copied the sentence onto her phone, under her deleted drafts. Then she rewrote it in her own words, because "I felt stuck" sounded like a poster in a counselor's office. "I sat up until one with nothing to build from. Can you send them to me by nine tomorrow?" She read it aloud, quiet, under the engine noise.

"That's not an accusation," Katherine said. "That's a weather report. Things that happened to a person."

The bus lurched around the depot corner, and Kayson was three rows back with his headphones half on, watching the window like it owed him something. Jade stood, gripping the rail, and went to him. He pulled out one earbud when he saw her, and his shoulders went up before she'd said a word, bracing for the thing she wasn't going to say.

"Hey," she said. "I'm not mad. I sat up until one with nothing to build from, and I felt kind of stuck. Can you get them to me by nine tomorrow? I'll fix the eagles."

"The eagles are terrible," he agreed, and something in his face loosened, like he'd been carrying the apology around all day with nowhere to put it. "Nine's fine. I couldn't do the graphs, though. I don't get the graphs."

"I'll do the graphs. You do the timeline." She sat down across the aisle, already opening her notebook on her knee, and Katherine caught her eye from two seats up and lifted the notebook page with Gordon's sentence on it, just slightly, like a referee signaling a fair play.

At the next stop the rain had thinned to a drizzle, and Jade texted her mother that she'd be home late, then wrote, beneath the message to Kayson that she'd finally sent: thank you for not making me pretend it was fine.

He looked at his phone, then at her, and put the earbud back in without answering, but he was smiling at the window when the bus pulled out.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
The piano arrived on a Tuesday, secondhand from an estate sale, and by Thursday Michael had counted the keys twice. Eighty-eight in all, fifty-two white and thirty-six black, a fact he confirmed by marking a pencil tick on a scrap of paper every time his finger crossed from one octave to the next. His mother had said the piano would inculcate discipline in him, using the word the way she used words like that, as if naming a virtue could install it, and he had not argued because the piano had cost less than a semester of the lessons he was about to stop being able to afford.

He was alone with it now, on a Saturday morning in the living room where the blinds cut the light into slats across the lid. Ms. Sánchez, the neighbour two floors down who had played professionally in another country, had agreed to listen to him once a month, and his first visit was tomorrow. The piece was a short Chopin prelude, the melancholic one in E minor, chosen from a library book because it looked simple and was not. The problem was the middle section, where the left hand jumped in a pattern his fingers refused to hold, and he had been stuck on the same eight bars for six days.

He played the bars again and dropped the ending again, and the silence afterward had the flat taste of failure. In the flashback that came to him then he was eleven, sitting on Rayden's basement floor while Rayden's older cousin played the same prelude without looking at her hands. Michael had asked her how many keys there were, thinking that a savant would know without counting, and she had laughed and said she'd never counted, that knowing the number wouldn't help him play. He had thought that was a dodge, a secret kept. Now, with the number counted and memorized, he was beginning to suspect she'd been telling the truth, and that the counting had been a way of touching the instrument without having to play it.

He tried the passage slower. Then slower still, so slow the notes stopped being music and became separate events, like footsteps on stairs in the dark. At that speed his left hand found the jumps, and he understood something his mother's word discipline had never covered: the slow speed was not a step toward the fast one, it was the fast one, unfolded. He kept at it, bar by bar, and when he brought the tempo up, his hand missed once, then held.

The doorbell rang mid-phrase. It was Hannah, holding a phone out already recording, because Rayden had told her Michael had a piano now and she wanted proof. He let her in and she stood by the window while he played the passage for her, not the whole piece, just the eight bars he'd conquered, and she lowered the phone without pressing stop.

"Your left hand is doing something and your right hand is doing something else," she said. "Like two people."

"It's fifty-two white keys and thirty-six black ones," he said, because that was what he said when he didn't know what else to say about it. "Eighty-eight total. I counted."

Hannah looked at him the way the cousin had looked at him five years ago, half amusement, half something softer. "Okay," she said. "Play the rest. I'll sit."

He told her the rest wasn't ready, and that was true, and then he started from the beginning anyway, because that was also true, and the opening came out cleaner than it had any right to, the melody settling into the room like dust that had finally found the floor. At the middle section he did not slow down. His hand jumped, held, jumped again. He felt the exact moment his attention leaned forward ahead of the notes, wanting the ending before it arrived, and the third jump slipped, a wrong key in the bass, black where white should have been. He kept playing. The wrong note made a chord nobody had written, low and strange under the melody, and it passed, and the piece closed the way the piece closes, quiet and unfinished-sounding even though it was over.

Hannah said, "Do it again."

"Tomorrow," he said. "I have the lesson tomorrow. Ms. Sánchez, downstairs." He lifted his hands off the keys and looked at them, at the fingers that had lied to him for six days and told the truth for four minutes. Outside, a bus went by, and the piano held the last of its sound under the hum.

"One more time," Hannah said, and sat down on the floor beside the bench, phone still recording, screen tilted up at him.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The letter from Stillwater College sat in the middle of the kitchen table, thin enough that Emma could tell before opening it that it was not a fat envelope, and everyone knew the fat envelopes were the good ones. Mandy had come over the moment Emma texted her, arriving with two hot chocolates and an expression that kept switching between encouragement and apology, as if she had rehearsed both on the walk and could not decide which to wear.

"You have to open it," Mandy said, sliding one cup across the table. "Or I can read it to you. I'll transcribe it into normal words. 'Congratulations' stays 'congratulations.' 'Unfortunately' becomes 'their loss.'"

Emma turned the envelope over twice, then set it down beside the practice test she had been reviewing, the one with the math section circled in red. "After this," she said. "I want to figure out what happened on the SAT first, while the wait is still mine."

The wait had been ten weeks since the test, and the strange thing was that she had walked out of the testing center almost cheerful, until the math. The first module had felt fair, almost easy, and then the second had opened with a question about an annuity, payments and interest over years, the kind of thing her father talked about at dinner when he was worried about money. She had stared at it, then at the next one, harder still, and somewhere in the middle of the second module a cold certainty had settled on her: she had been routed into the stupid questions, the ones they gave you when the machine had already decided you were hopeless.

She told Mandy this now, working her thumbnail along the envelope's seam without tearing it. "The whole second half was brutal. It kept getting harder, like the test was punishing me for guessing on the first part."

Mandy frowned into her hot chocolate. "Wait. Harder?" She pulled out her phone, typed, scrolled, and turned the screen around. "Kale sent me this article after his test. The SAT went digital last March, and it's adaptive. How you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second module. So if your second module was hard..."

Emma looked at the screen. Adaptive. The first module had felt easy because she had done well on it, and the machine had handed her the harder questions because it thought she could carry them. She sat back in the kitchen chair so fast that it creaked.

"I spent three weeks thinking I bombed it," she said. "I told my dad I was looking at community college. He got so quiet about it. He started pricing out this annuity thing, some safe investment he said would cover a trade school, and I let him believe it because I thought the score was already lost."

Flashback: the night after the scores were scheduled to come out and didn't, her father at this same table with his calculator and his coffee going cold, drawing little boxes and arrows on a napkin, showing her how money could be steady and boring and still add up to something. He had looked so tired and so careful with her, like she was made of the same thin paper as the rejection letters he assumed were coming. She had said "maybe I'm not a college person" just to make the conversation smaller, and he had nodded slowly, and she had hated herself for the relief on his face, as if one more weight had been lifted off a man already carrying too many.

"That's not the same as knowing I did well," Emma said now, slowly, because she wanted to be honest with Mandy and with herself. "Harder questions probably mean I earned them. But I could still have choked on all of them. I could have gotten the hard questions and missed every single one." She turned the phone back toward Mandy. "It's a better theory than mine. It's not an answer."

"Which is why," Mandy said, tapping the envelope, "you open that. Answers are literally their business."

Emma picked it up. The paper tore cleanly. Inside was one page, and her eyes went to the middle of the paragraph before she could stop them, and then she read the words "waitlist" and felt something complicated unfold in her chest, hope and postponement braided together, and she pushed the page across the table so Mandy could see it too.

"Waitlisted," Mandy read out loud. "That's not a no. That's a maybe with a waiting room." She was already reaching for her phone to text Kale, whose cousin had gotten off a waitlist two years ago, and Emma picked up her hot chocolate with both hands and held it against her chin, looking at the word on the page.

"Dad's going to want to frame this," she said. "He frames everything."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958; the resulting graph is called the Keeling Curve.
story:
Grandpa's study smelled of pencil shavings and the pipe he had given up years ago, and Luke spread his materials across the desk where the afternoon light fell in a long stripe. He had volunteered for the hardest section of the class presentation, the science part, mostly because Camilla had said, half laughing, that nobody else wanted it. Ms. Dhillon wanted them to explain not just that the climate was warming but how anyone actually knew, which meant graphs, which meant Luke had to understand them well enough to stand in front of thirty people and not sound like he was reading a cereal box.

The graph itself was famous, the rising zigzag line that every documentary used, but its origin kept sliding away from him. He had the picture saved on his laptop and the numbers it implied, and he could explain in general terms how greenhouse gases let sunlight in and slow heat on its way back out, how the molecules absorb infrared radiation and re-emit it, some of it downward. What he could not find, after an hour of searching, was the name of the place where the measurements came from. His notes just said "a station in Hawaii," which felt like citing "a hospital in Europe" for a medical discovery.

He called Dominik, who was handling the economics section and was, as always, cheerful about things Luke found grim. Dominik's part was about how a town goes under when its main employer leaves, how insolvency spreads from the mill to the shops to the families, and he kept insisting that Luke's science section had to be airtight before anyone would listen to the money part. "People discount the whole argument if you get one detail wrong," Dominik said. "My dad does it constantly. He finds a typo and declares the whole magazine fraudulent."

"You're the one always saying people can't be reasoned into caring," Luke said.

"I'm saying you can't disenfranchise them with jargon and then wonder why they stop listening." Dominik hung up on that, cheerfully, the way he ended most calls, and Luke sat looking at the desk his grandfather had built by hand out of wood salvaged from a boreal forest cabin the family had lost before Luke was born. Grandpa never called it a loss. He called it a trade. The cabin for the education of his children, which had worked out, more or less, though nobody in the family agreed on whether it had been worth it, and Grandpa himself would say only that it depended on which decade you asked him in.

Grandpa came in with two cups of tea, set one down on a coaster he had made from the same wood, and looked over Luke's shoulder. Luke explained the problem, the graph, the missing name, and Grandpa said nothing for a while, which was his way of listening. Then he said, "When I was your age, nobody measured that at all. Somebody had to start. Look for who started, not where."

Luke went back to it with a different search, the man instead of the place, and there it was: Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, who had begun regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958. The graph that came out of it was called the Keeling Curve. Luke wrote the name down twice, once in his notes and once on the back of his hand, because it felt like the kind of thing that would evaporate under pressure.

Camilla texted him a photograph of her section, the boreal forests burning in the north, orange against grey sky, and asked whether it was too much. He typed that it was exactly enough, then deleted that and typed that it was honest, then deleted that too and just sent back a thumbs up, and wondered which version she would have preferred. He was still deciding about the whole presentation, honestly. Dominik thought you led with numbers because numbers could not be argued with. Camilla thought you led with images because people argued with numbers all day. Luke had started to think both were right and that the order mattered less than the admitting, out loud, that the zigzag line was measured by one stubborn man on one volcano starting in March 1958, that it was a record and not a prophecy, and that a record was still something you could trust.

Grandpa drifted back in near dusk and read the notes over Luke's shoulder again, tapping the page where Luke had written the station's name. "Mauna Loa," Grandpa said, as if confirming he'd heard it right. "A volcano. Good place for a beginning." He picked up his tea and stood by the window while the light went from gold to grey over the yard, and outside the wind moved through the maples the way it had moved through them every summer Luke could remember, indifferent to what anyone had measured.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around Evan's arm until it squeezed like a hand closing, then released in slow, glacial stages while the numbers on the little screen climbed and fell. He had borrowed the machine from Ms. Demir, the retired nurse in 3B, after she found him standing in the hallway outside her door holding a casserole dish his mother had sent down and not knowing what to say past thank you. Ms. Demir had said, "For your father, then," and gone inside and come back with the monitor in a zippered case, and had not asked him anything else, which he was grateful for.

His father was coming home on Thursday. Six weeks since the stroke, six weeks of the hospital and then the rehabilitation wing, and the discharge papers listed things to watch for, and near the top of the list was blood pressure. Evan had read the phrase a hundred times without knowing what to do with it. Numbers on a page were one thing. A machine in his hands, in this kitchen where his father would sit tomorrow morning expecting breakfast, was another.

Laila came over after school because she was the one in their health class who actually read the textbook instead of skimming the bolded parts. She set her bag on the counter and pulled out the chapter they'd been assigned. "Okay," she said. "You hold the arm still, I'll read the screen." Evan slid the cuff higher on his own arm, because he wanted to practice on himself before he practiced on anyone who mattered. The machine inflated, deflated, and settled on a pair of numbers: 118 over 76.

"Is that good?" he asked. Laila turned pages, frowning at the table in the chapter. "Under the 2017 guideline it's normal," she said. "Normal is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. So you're under both." Evan looked at the screen a long moment. He had expected to feel relieved, and instead he felt something more like suspicion, as if the numbers were being kind to him the way people had been kind to him since March, in a way that made him want to check their math.

"Then why did it happen to him," Evan said. It wasn't a question and Laila didn't treat it as one. She turned to the section on family history instead. "Genetics counts," she said. "Consanguinity, shared blood, that raises some risks. It's in the chapter. It doesn't decide anything by itself, though. It's one factor among the diet stuff and the exercise stuff." Evan had wanted to believe, for six weeks, in a single cause, something he could point at and remove, and her voice disabused him of that gently, without ceremony, the way she corrected lab reports.

He took his own reading twice more, then wrote both sets of numbers in a notebook with the date, because the chapter said patterns mattered more than single readings. Then he read the diet pages out loud while Laila chopped the cucumber she'd found in the fridge, because she'd said she was hungry and had simply started making a salad for both of them without asking. He read about sodium and about walking, thirty minutes most days, and he thought about his father's mornings, the deli coffee, the eggs, the car pulling out of the lot at work. He thought about how he could not remake another person's habits, only set the table differently and walk beside him.

"It's not a promise," he said. "Right? Like, the numbers can be normal and something still happens, or they can be high and nothing happens for thirty years." Laila considered it, chewing. "That's what the chapter says, basically. It's about probability. They can't tell you your future, only your odds." Evan nodded slowly. It was an uncomfortable kind of knowledge, the kind that gave you something to do but no guarantee that doing it would be enough, and he decided he would rather hold it honestly than swap it for a comfortable story.

On Thursday morning his father sat in the chair by the window with his left hand curled loosely in his lap, the side that was still slow to answer him. Evan set down the oatmeal, waited until his father had tasted it and pronounced it, with narrowed eyes, better than expected, and then brought out the machine and the notebook. "They want us to check it," Evan said, sliding the cuff up his father's good arm. "I've been practicing. I'll write it down every time." His father looked at the machine, then at the notebook with its columns of dates and numbers, then at his son. "Go on then," he said, and held out his arm.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point.
story:
Savannah had agreed to housesit for her grandmother for one week, and she had promised herself she would use the quiet to pass the calculus placement test that would let her skip the first semester of math in college. She was not sure the promise had been wise. At home, with Jadyn texting her jokes and Presley dropping by unannounced, she had managed to study for forty minutes at a stretch. Here, in her grandmother's kitchen, with the clock ticking in the hallway and the hydrangeas pressing against the window, she had run out of excuses, and it unsettled her to discover that the silence was harder company than her friends.

The textbook was her mother's, secondhand, its margins annotated in faded pencil by some stranger. She had reached the section on derivatives of polynomials three days ago and stalled there, copying the power rule without believing it. Bring the exponent down, subtract one. Fine for x squared, which became two x. But when she tried the practice problem, a function modeling the volume of a box she was supposed to maximize, the arithmetic kept slipping away from her, and yesterday she had thrown her pencil across the kitchen and felt peevish about it for an hour.

She had not told anyone she was doing this. Her counselor had signed the form without comment, but Ms. Wilson, her junior-year teacher, had frowned when Savannah mentioned it in the spring. "You're disenfranchising yourself from the whole first-year experience," Ms. Wilson had said, half teasing, and Savannah had argued back that skipping a course she could test out of was not the same as skipping a course she needed. She still thought she was right. She also still heard the frown.

This morning she spread graph paper across the kitchen table and drew the function for the box problem, plotting points one by one, connecting them into a curve that rose, leveled somewhere near x equals four, and fell again. Somewhere in that flat region was the maximum, the biggest volume, the point she was hunting. She could see it. She could not calculate it. The power rule gave her a formula for the derivative, three x squared minus twenty-four x plus forty-eight, but the formula sat on the page like a stranger's handwriting, unconnected to the hill she had drawn.

She called Jadyn, who was in math club and had taken the test last year. "Bring the function down to something you can see," Jadyn said over the phone, munching something. "I used to lay a ruler along the curve. Where the curve tops out, flat, the ruler lies flat too. That's what the derivative gives you, the slope of the tangent line at that point. You set the derivative to zero because zero slope is flat." Savannah wrote the last part down while Jadyn described a party she was missing by studying, and its detractors, who claimed the whole event was an excuse for one girl's boyfriend to show off his car.

Savannah hung up and set the derivative equal to zero. Three x squared minus twenty-four x plus forty-eight equals zero became, after division and the quadratic formula she had to redo twice, x equals two or x equals six. Two answers. She laid the ruler against her curve at x equals two and found the curve still climbing there, the ruler tilting upward, and at x equals six she found it falling, the ruler tipped down. Neither was flat. She sat back, certain she had failed, and nearly closed the notebook before an older suspicion surfaced: her plotted curve might be wrong. She had been sloppy, connecting dots too loosely, rounding values. The arithmetic of the derivative was the part she trusted least, and yet it was her drawing that had lied.

She replotted the function carefully, point by point, checking each value twice, and the new curve crested neatly at x equals four. At four, she laid the ruler along the paper and it lay level, touching the curve at its summit, no tilt in either direction. Between the two roots, two and six, the crest sat exactly at the midpoint, and she understood, in a way that felt physical rather than verbal, that the formula and the ruler were describing the same fact in two languages. Plugging four back into the original function gave the maximum volume, and she checked that number against her graph and found them agreeing within the width of her pencil line.

She thought about Ms. Wilson's frown again, sitting there with the ruler still resting on the paper. Maybe the first-year course taught this the slow way, with the reasoning she had just shortchanged. Maybe she had only learned to compute, not to understand, and the placement test would not ask her the difference. She copied the maximum volume onto a clean page and underlined it twice, then carried her grandmother's watering can out to the hydrangeas, where the afternoon light had gone long and low across the porch boards.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 10.0 percent of wage and salary workers were union members in 2025, down from 20.1 percent in 1983.
story:
The ticket printer spat out an order for two beet salads and a salmon, and Autumn pinned it above the station without looking at the clock, which was a mistake, because the clock was the whole argument. Nine forty-eight. Her shift, according to the schedule taped inside the pantry door, ended at nine. Ms. Li had left an hour ago, and the closing manager, a man everyone called Boss only partly as a joke, stood at the pass with his arms folded, watching the last tables of the dining room like weather coming in.

"Autumn, stay till close," he said. "Big party walked in. I'll square it with you next week, cash."

She had learned what "square it with you" meant in her four months at the Garden Gate. It meant the hours vanished from the payroll system, and the cash arrived sometimes, folded into her apron pocket, untracked and untaxed and always less than time-and-a-half would have been. She was sixteen and needed the money for a laptop before fall semester, and the needing made every decision heavier, because a person who needs the job cannot easily be a person who questions it.

Stefan, who was eighteen and had worked line jobs since he was fifteen, caught her eye across the sauté station. He shook his head once, a small motion, almost nothing. Later, scraping down the flat top while the dish machine hissed behind them, he said, "At my uncle's hotel there's a contract. Breaks written in, overtime written in. Stuff you don't have to ask for because it's already on paper."

"Like rules?"

"Like codified," Stefan said. "Written down so nobody can unwrite it by being in a bad mood." He snapped a towel at the steam rising off the grill, and the steam shredded and reformed, and neither of them said anything else, because the closing manager was walking back through the kitchen.

She stayed until eleven forty. On the bus home she texted Eshal, who was doing a project for their economics class and had asked everyone she knew to interview a family member about their working life. Autumn had put it off for two weeks, and now, with her feet aching against the floor of the bus, she remembered that her grandmother had worked summers at a cannery back in the early eighties, before she emigrated. She texted: can I interview you about your old job? not for gossip, for class. The reply came as a voice note, and then, because her grandmother distrusted anything that could be accidentally deleted, a letter arrived on Sunday, folded into a card with a blue heron on it.

The letter sat on Autumn's desk beside the anthropology of her own room: textbooks, a mug of cold tea, laundry in a soft grey landslide. Her grandmother wrote in careful looped cursive that in her cannery summer nearly everyone she worked beside carried a union card, and that when the line speeds got cruel, a man named Mr. Okafor walked to the office with four others and came back saying the speeds would stay where they were, and by Monday they stayed. She wrote that half the country seemed to belong to unions in those years, or close to it, and that she had been proud to pay the small deduction, proud in a way Autumn would have to take on faith, because it was not the kind of pride that photographs well. At the bottom she added, in smaller handwriting: You asked once why I always read my pay stub. Now you know.

Autumn did what she always did with a claim she could not verify: she looked it up. Not the memory of the cannery, which was hers and unprovable, but the numbers underneath it. The Bureau of Labor Statistics kept the figures, and she found them on her phone, squinting at the small screen in the kitchen light she should have turned off already. Twenty point one percent of wage and salary workers were union members in 1983. Ten point zero percent in 2025. She read it twice, then a third time, as though the second decimal might shift if she waited. Half, her grandmother had guessed, glancing from memory toward a statistic, and she had landed closer than Autumn would have guessed, and farther from the present than Autumn wanted to believe. Her whole kitchen, everyone she had ever worked with at the Garden Gate, existed inside that shrunken number, inside rooms where nothing was codified and everything was arranged person by person, mood by mood.

On Monday she told Stefan at the staff meal, over the free bowls of pasta the restaurant offered in place of, among other things, a lot of other things. "I looked it up. Twenty point one percent of workers were union members in 1983. Now it's ten point zero. Exactly half, basically. Since my grandma started working." She pushed the salt across the table to him. "So when Boss says stay late and I stay late, that's not just my problem. It's a whole shape."

Stefan twirled his fork. "It's entropy," he said. "Not the physics kind. The everything-slowly-falls-apart kind. Every job a little worse than the last one, and nobody notices because it happened one Saturday at a time." He was joking a little, the way people joke about weather they cannot change, but he kept looking at her, waiting to see whether she would laugh too.

She thought about Mr. Okafor walking to the office with four others. She thought about the laptop, and about how the cash in her apron pocket on Saturday had been twenty dollars short of what the hours were worth, and about how she had said thank you. There was a version of the next Saturday where she said something else, where she said, put it in the system, and a version where she said nothing again, and she could not yet see which version she was. Maybe both lived in her the way the two numbers lived in one chart, one falling away from the other, and maybe the distance between them was just the size of a girl deciding. She did not know. She knew only that her grandmother read every pay stub, and that this was a thing a person could inherit without ever being told to.

The printer chirped. Two beet salads, one salmon, and, at the bottom of the ticket in the manager's cramped capitals, STAY TILL CLOSE.

Autumn looked at the clock, then at Stefan, then at the ticket spinning slightly on its pin.

"Put it in the system," she said, out loud, to the kitchen.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
The lantern lay folded on Avery's lap like a failed origami crane, its seams gaping where she had pressed too hard. Her aunt's car smelled of incense and old vinyl, and outside the window the streets of the town slid past, hung with paper decorations that had been up for days. In the back seat beside her, Maelle was quiet for once, watching the same streets, and in the front her aunt drove with both hands on the wheel the way people do when they are carrying something careful.

"You could take another one," her aunt said, glancing at the mirror. "There are spares at the river."

"I want this one." Avery turned the lantern over. It had a tear along one fold, and she had tried to suture it with a strip of tape that now curled at the edges. She had made it three days ago at the community hall, on her second evening in Japan, before she had understood what any of it was for. She had thought it was a craft activity. She had thought a lot of things were craft activities that first week.

Her grandfather had died in March, in a hospital she had never visited, in a town she had never seen until June. Her mother had flown over twice that year and come back each time with less to say. Avery had known him through a video call every New Year, eleven minutes long, mostly her grandfather watching her while her mother translated. When the school year ended, her mother had said go, and she had gone, and now it was August, and the whole town was preparing for something her aunt called Obon.

"It's Obon," her aunt had said on the first night, standing in the doorway of the old house while down the street a small fire burned in a clay basin, and neighbours were kneeling around it. "We light the fires to welcome them home." She had not said who them was. She had not needed to. Avery had stood at that fire with her aunt and her mother and felt the heat on her shins and understood, without anyone explaining, that the heat was meant for someone arriving.

That was the part that had unsettled her. Welcoming implied a relationship, a history of arrivals, and she had none. Her grandfather was a man who had once mailed her a pencil case with a cat on it and had written, in careful English on the card, that he hoped she was studying well. Eleven minutes a year. She had sat at the welcome fire anyway, because her mother was crying quietly beside her and it seemed worse to sit apart.

"You're doing that thing," Maelle said now, in the back seat, nodding at the lantern. "Where you stare at something like it owes you money."

"It's ripped. It's going to sink."

"So it sinks. Everything sinks eventually." Maelle had come over for the summer on a language program and had attached herself to Avery's family with the confidence of someone who had read about the customs in a guidebook. "My physics teacher calls it entropy. Everything runs down. Even lanterns."

"That's not comforting."

"It wasn't meant to be. It was meant to be true." Maelle peeled the tape strip off and smoothed it back over the tear, pressing with her thumbnail until it held. "There. Now it's only mostly doomed."

The car slowed and joined a line of others heading toward the river, headlights doubling on the wet asphalt. Ahead, Avery could see people walking with lanterns held out from their bodies, the paper glowing faintly from within where candles had already been lit, and the whole procession looked diaphanous in the dusk, like something seen through frosted glass. Her aunt parked beneath a bridge, and they walked the last stretch along the bank, where the river moved slow and dark and full already of small lights drifting out toward the sea.

Avery crouched at the water's edge with her torn lantern and the candle her mother handed her. She thought about how little she knew, how eleven minutes a year was not enough to grieve on, and how the fire and the river were doing something her own mind could not: making a shape for it. She would go home in ten days and start college and the distance would close over this summer like water over a stone. That was a loss, she decided, but not only a loss. She had come, and she had lit the welcome fire, and now she would do the last part, which everyone here knew and no one had lectured her about: at the end of Obon the lanterns went down the river to guide the spirits back, and then the town would put out its fires and go inside.

She set the lantern on the surface and let go of the rim. It listed, took on a little water through the taped seam, and then steadied, spinning slowly until its light faced back toward the bank. Her mother's hand found her shoulder. Maelle was already filming it on her phone, and her aunt stood with her arms folded, watching the light shrink downstream. "Wait," Avery said, and knelt and pushed the lantern gently with two fingers, sending it out to join the others, its small flame riding the dark water toward the sea.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java fields left uninitialized get default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, and null for object references.
story:
The basement smelled like dryer sheets and cold pizza, and Sidney's laptop sat open on the ping-pong table between three folding chairs. Sierra pulled her own computer out of her bag and set it down beside the sticky note Sidney had stuck to the netless table that read, in aggressive capital letters, DO NOT SPILL. "Okay," Sidney said, clapping once. "Book class. Private fields. Getters. You wanted to learn it before Monday, so we're learning it."

Sierra had her reasons, and she'd rehearsed them on the walk over. Mr. Navarro had posted the first real assignment of the semester, due in six days, and she'd spent two years letting other people write the parts of her projects that touched Java. Frances, cross-legged on an old couch cushion with a biology textbook, glanced up long enough to say that Sierra was being dramatic, and Sierra said she was being strategic, which was different. She wanted to build something that ran because she had built it, not because she'd stood behind Sidney at the keyboard saying "wait, no, try the other bracket" until something worked.

They started with the fields. Sidney typed fast and narrated faster, and Sierra made her slow down and go back. Private title. Private pages. Private checkedOut, which was a boolean, which Frances said was a fancy word for a yes-or-no question, and Sidney said it was just a light switch with a college degree. Then the constructor, then the getter methods, one for each field, each one nothing more than a return statement wearing a small formal hat. Sierra copied the shape of it into her own file, retyping every line herself even when Sidney offered to just share the document, because the point, she had decided somewhere on the walk over, was to have it in her hands.

The tests came next. Sidney showed her how to write a main method that built a Book and printed what the getters handed back, and Sierra ran hers and the console offered up its verdict: the title printed as null. Not an error, not a blank, but the word itself, lowercase and unbothered, sitting in the output like it had every right to be there. "What is that," Sierra said, not a question, more an accusation. "That's not empty, that's null."

Sidney leaned over, read her code, and started laughing in a way that promised nothing helpful. "You never set the title in your constructor. You made the field and then you just. Didn't." Frances put down her biology book and said that in genetics it would be like having the genotype for a trait and never expressing it, all the instructions and no phenotype, and Sidney said Frances was not allowed to make the computer sound cool tonight because it was Sierra's turn. But Sierra was staring at the output, and something was assembling itself. "So if I don't put anything in a field," she said slowly, "Java puts something in anyway." Sidney shrugged. "Numbers get zero. Booleans get false." Sierra looked back at the screen. "And anything that's not a number or a yes-or-no gets null. Like the title."

She tested it, because that was the other thing she was learning, that you didn't have to take anyone's word for anything. She made a second Book without going through the constructor at all, printed the pages, and got 0. Printed the checkedOut, and got false. Printed the title, and got null again, patient as ever. Frances came over and looked at the three lines of output and said it was weirdly tidy, like the language refused to leave a room empty, and Sierra said she couldn't decide if that was considerate or lazy, and Sidney said it was both, like most things.

At half past ten Frances drafted a message to Mr. Navarro, because Frances drafted everything, and read it aloud for approval. "Dear Mr. Navarro. I hope your weekend is going better than your mood on Friday, which was irascible even by your standards. Question from the basement study group: if a field is never initialized, does the language guarantee the default, or is that just what the compiler does when it's feeling generous? We will accept your judgment as final, as you remind us yours always is. P.S. Sierra wrote her own class from scratch and only blamed the computer twice." Frances offered to send it, and Sierra said yes, and then said wait, and then said send it, and then put her forehead briefly on the table next to the sticky note.

What she hadn't said out loud, in the basement or on the walk home afterward, was that she still couldn't adjudicate between the two versions of herself: the one who wanted to know exactly why the language behaved the way it did, mechanism and reason, and the one who thought you could build plenty of true things on top of rules you'd verified without fully understanding. The message from Mr. Navarro was waiting when she got home, one line long. "Guaranteed. Read the spec, not the mood. And tell Sierra the third blame was her best one." She laughed once, alone in her kitchen, then opened the file and changed the constructor so the title could never come back null again, and ran the test to watch it print the name she'd given it.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
Isabelle had agreed to light the menorah before she understood what agreeing would mean. The festival committee wanted a teenager from the synagogue to do the public lighting on the fourth night, and her mother had volunteered her with a cheerful ruthlessness, the way she volunteered Isabelle for everything, as though enthusiasm were a trait that could be assigned like a chore. Now Isabelle stood behind the folding table near the stage, where a menorah the size of a small child waited on a plywood base, and tried to remember which candles to use.

"You look like you're about to defuse something," said Amari, who had come to sell earrings at her aunt's jewelry stall and had abandoned it the moment she spotted Isabelle's face. Amari knew nothing about Hanukkah except that Isabelle missed school for it sometimes, and she watched now with open, unembarrassed curiosity, which was easier to bear than sympathy.

"Four nights," Isabelle said. "It's the fourth night, so four candles. Plus the one that lights them." She counted the arms of the menorah with her eyes and came up with a number she didn't expect. She counted again. Nine. She stood very still, because if she moved she might have to admit out loud that she had never actually counted before, that in eleven years of watching her father light the menorah at home she had never once tallied the branches.

"You need five and you've got nine?" Amari said. "That's not a crisis, that's arithmetic."

"It's not arithmetic," Isabelle said, and then, because that sounded rude and untrue, "It's both." What she couldn't say was that the extra branches felt like a door she'd walked past a thousand times without opening. She thought of the rabbi's son at Hebrew school, the one who used to say that if you couldn't explain a holiday to a stranger, you didn't really know it yourself. She had always thought he was a charlatan, honestly, a boy who performed seriousness the way other boys performed indifference. She was beginning to suspect he'd been right, which was worse.

Ms. Warsame, who taught world history at the high school and lived two houses down from Isabelle's grandmother, appeared beside the table with a paper cup of cider and no visible hurry. "Are you the one lighting tonight?" she asked. "I came early on purpose. I've never seen it done." Her fourth-period class had argued about whether holidays survived translation or got flattened by it, whether something ritual could be transliterated into a new language, letter by letter, and still carry its weight. Isabelle had gotten a B minus on that essay, for being, in Ms. Warsame's incisive red ink, "ambitious but not yet willing to choose a side."

"The middle one," Isabelle said suddenly, mostly to herself. The ninth branch stood taller than the rest, set apart. She could see it now that she was actually looking, the way the structure had been there the whole time, one helper and eight for the nights, the helper taller so it stood over the others. "The tall one in the middle. My dad calls it the shamash." She had heard the word a hundred times without asking what it did, and now, saying it to Amari and Ms. Warsame, she understood it as she spoke: the helper candle, the one that lights the others and then stands there, burning for everyone.

From across the square, Amari watched her friend's shoulders settle before the announcer called her name. Amari had sold four pairs of earrings since noon and would hear about it from her aunt later, but she found she couldn't leave. Isabelle climbed the two steps to the stage, took the long taper from a woman in a windbreaker, and lit the shamash first. Then, holding it, she touched four flames into being, one for each night, her hand steadier than it had been all evening. Below the stage a boy from her chemistry class, Tommy, called out, "Fourth night!" as though he were calling a race, and people laughed, and Isabelle laughed too.

She turned to the crowd with the helper candle still in her hand. "This one's the shamash," she said into the microphone. "It lights the others." Ms. Warsame raised her paper cup. Amari cupped her hands around her mouth and shouted, "That's my friend up there," and the wax ran warm between Isabelle's fingers as she set the candle, still burning, back in its tall place among the eight.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Research by linguist Paul Nation and colleagues suggests readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help.
story:
The article had come from a stack of yellowing newspapers in his grandfather's back room, and even in the first paragraph Antoine could feel it resisting him. The headline, at least, was legible: something about a small town in Provence and its annual festival of olives. His grandfather had set the paper on the kitchen table that morning with a look of ceremony, the way other grandfathers presented fishing rods or old watches, and Antoine had promised, before he understood what he was promising, that he would read one article and tell him, in French, what it said.

He sat now at the same table with the window open to the garden, where his grandfather was pruning the fig tree with slow, deliberate cuts. The kitchen smelled of coffee and thyme. In the first paragraph alone Antoine counted eleven words he did not know, and this was supposed to be a short article, barely a column. He could subsume some of them under guesses: "arboriculteur" was probably a grower of some kind, since the sentence went on about trees, and "récolte" had to mean harvest because of the baskets mentioned after it. But the guesses stacked up, and by the second paragraph he was constructing the meaning out of almost nothing, like a builder who had been handed every third brick.

His phone buzzed twice on the table. Kash had sent him a photograph of the lake where he, Camron and half their class had gone that weekend, Camron midair above the water in an ungraceful but committed dive. You missing this, Kash had written, and Antoine had typed "sort of" and then deleted it, because it was tautological to say he was both there in the photo and not, and anyway his grandfather's house had its own arguments to make. He set the phone face down and tried the third paragraph again.

It was about a man, an older grower, who had won first prize for his oil three years running, and who described, in a quotation Antoine had to read four times, the difference between an oil that was merely good and one that was unforgettable. The word the man used was "épicurien," and Antoine, after a moment, heard it open: the old grower was calling himself an epicure, someone for whom eating was a matter of refined pleasure rather than fuel. That single word unlocked the whole sentence, and for a moment the paragraph was not a puzzle but a portrait, a fussy old man with strong opinions about bitterness and grassiness and the color of the first pressing.

Then the fourth paragraph closed over him again. Words like "amertume" and "terroir" and something about "macération" that he could not even guess at. He counted again, honestly this time, marking the unknown words with small pencil dots. Out of roughly a hundred and fifty words in the article, he counted a little more than twenty he could not get, even generously. That was more like one in seven, and he sat back and looked at the dots and felt the shape of the problem for the first time, not as a failure of effort but as arithmetic.

He took out his phone, this time to search, typing carefully: how many words do you need to know to read a text without help. The answer that surfaced was from a linguist named Paul Nation, whose research with colleagues suggested that readers needed to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help. Antoine looked at his dotted column and did the math. He was somewhere in the mid-eighties. He was not lazy and he was not stupid; he had simply chosen, or been handed, an article that sat beyond the threshold where reading stopped being reading and became decoding.

He thought about Mr. Castillo, who had told them in Spanish class that the point of a summary was not to translate everything but to say what mattered. At the time it had sounded like a way of lowering the bar. Now it seemed like a different thing entirely, a division of labor: the words he did know could carry the outline, and the ones he did not could be admitted as gaps, named as gaps, instead of papered over with guesses. He wrote four sentences on the back of a grocery receipt, in French, crossing out and rewriting, and then walked out to the garden holding the newspaper like a script.

His grandfather stopped pruning and listened, shears in one hand, while Antoine said that the article was about a festival, and about a man who had won three years in a row, and that the man believed a truly great oil was a question of pleasure, of taste pursued almost as an end in itself. Antoine paused and then, because the whole exercise was worthless if he hid the gaps, added: "Il y a des mots que je ne connais pas. Des détails sur la fabrication."

His grandfather nodded slowly, not correcting anything, and set the shears down on the wall. He asked, in English, whether Antoine had liked the old grower or found him insufferable. Antoine laughed, caught off guard, and said he had liked him, mostly. His grandfather said, "Then tomorrow you will read the paragraph about him again, and you will tell me what he said about the bitterness," and picked the shears back up. A green fig, still hard and pale, sat in his palm where he had cut it from the branch, and he held it out across the garden for Antoine to see.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one; the tenancy continues month to month automatically on the same terms.
story:
The two leases arrived as scans in his grandfather's email, forwarded to Colton with the subject line "you're good at this" and nothing else. Colton printed them at the kitchen table because reading contracts on a screen felt like trying to swim in a bathtub. The first was the lease his grandfather had now, a one-bedroom in Owen Sound at nine hundred and eighty dollars a month, heat and water included, hydro billed separately at an average the old man had scrawled on a sticky note: sixty-one dollars. The second was the "renewal" the landlord wanted him to sign, eleven hundred and twenty, a full year's term, no utilities included.
