Colton made a grid in his notebook. He had learned grids from his mother, who delimited every decision in her life into columns, and he found it worked on problems the way salt worked on slugs. Rent, hydro, heating, water. The current lease, once you added the hydro, came to one thousand and forty-one a month. The new one, with heat and water and hydro all coming off a metered bill the landlord estimated "will vary," came to something north of thirteen hundred, depending on a winter nobody could price in advance.

"You're doing homework?" his mother asked, passing through with laundry.

"Grandpa's homework," Colton said. "He wants to know if he should sign."

She set the basket down. "He told me the landlord's been at him. Standing in the hallway with the papers already filled in."

"Nice guy," Colton said, which was the pithy version of a longer opinion he kept to himself.

He called Chance first, because Chance had moved twice in three years and considered himself a scholar of renting. Chance came over with his bike helmet still on and read both leases standing up, one hand on the table. "The second one's worse," he said. "Obviously. But if he doesn't sign, they evict him, right? That's why people sign."

"That's why people sign," Colton agreed, but he wrote it as a question in his notebook, because agreement with Chance had a poor track record. Curtis, when they looped him in over the phone, was no better. "My aunt got kicked out for not renewing," Curtis said. "Or she moved. One of those." Colton thanked him and hung up.

What he did next was the thing he did instead of asking an adult: he searched the leases' own language against the province's tenant board pages, reading until his eyes ached, following one thread after another. Somewhere between the sticky note and the fourth PDF, he found it, plain as a floor. When a fixed-term lease ends in Ontario, the tenant does not have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month, automatically, on the same terms. He read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to be arguing with everyone he knew. No new signature. Same rent, same conditions, rolling forward.

He called his grandfather. "Don't sign it," he said.

"I have to sign something, don't I? The year's up in June."

"No. That's the thing. When your lease ends, you don't have to sign a new one. It just goes month to month by itself, same terms. It's automatic."

There was a silence long enough that Colton checked the call hadn't dropped. "Month to month," his grandfather said slowly. "At the same rent."

"At the same rent. Same everything. You don't have to do anything."

"Huh," said his grandfather, and then, after another pause, "The landlord said I had to."

"He can want you to," Colton said. "Wanting isn't the same as having to."

His mother, listening from the doorway with a sock still in her hand, made a noise that was almost a laugh. "Your grandfather's been a reactionary his whole life," she said. "Whatever anyone proposes, he's against it. Now you've given him a reason."

Colton went back to his grid and added the fact to it in the margin, in small letters, like a load-bearing note. Then he sat with the numbers a while. If the tenancy rolled on at the same terms, the first column was the real one, one thousand and forty-one a month, and the second column was a choice, not a requirement. That was the part he hadn't understood at the start: he'd thought he was comparing two doors, and it turned out one of them was already open. Still, the landlord could apply to raise the rent, could find other ways to be unpleasant, and Colton wrote none of that down, because it was a shape of worry and not a number, and his grid held numbers. He texted his grandfather the total and the phrase month to month, and waited.

The reply came while he was washing the binder off his hands. "Told him I'm staying as I am. He didn't like it. I had the page printed before he left the hallway."

Colton read it twice, then propped the phone against the tap so his grandfather could watch him laugh.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, because the system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse.
story:
Charles had pinned the judging schedule to his corkboard three weeks earlier, and now the sheet hung above his kitchen table with one line circled twice: judges arrive at row six, 3:00. At 11:40 he stood in the gymnasium beside his contrivance, a sealed flask of cobalt solution wired to a heating coil and a thermometer, and watched the pink liquid fail to turn blue for the fourth time that morning.

His board read, in letters he had lettered carefully with a ruler: "Heating the flask will drive the reaction forward, producing more product." He had believed that on Tuesday. He had believed it all through spring break, when he'd stayed behind while his mother recuperated from her surgery and he'd built the coil from a dismantled hair dryer. Now the flask was warm to the touch and stubbornly, insultingly pink.

"Give it here," Imogen said. She was at the next table with her own project on water filtration, and she had wandered over during her slow stretches, the way she did, hands in her lab coat pockets. She held the flask up to the gymnasium fluorescents. "What colour is the product supposed to be?"

"Blue. It's blue in the cold, blue when I run it under the tap. Every time." He turned the coil off and pressed the flask against the cinder block wall, and within a minute the pink began to shade violet, then a deep, unmistakable blue. He stared at it. The heat was doing the opposite of what his board promised.

Spencer drifted over from the robotics table with a bag of chips, read the board, looked at the flask, and started laughing. "Your hypothesis is wrong in permanent marker."

"It's wrong," Charles said. His mouth was dry. There were three hours until the judges came, and his entire display, the nascent theory he'd been proud of a month ago, argued the wrong direction. He could take the board down and present the data honestly, or he could keep the flask cold all afternoon and hope nobody asked him to warm it.

He thought about Mr. Rossi, who taught chemistry and had signed his entry form without reading the hypothesis, the way he signed everything, rapidly, one eyebrow up. Charles had liked that about him. He had liked that nobody had checked his reasoning, because the reasoning had felt so obviously sound. Systems resisted change; that was the principle; you pushed heat in, and the reaction should push forward to use it. He'd rehearsed that sentence in the shower.

"Say it backwards," Imogen said. She was still holding the flask, turning it slowly, watching the last pink drain out of it. "Say what actually happens."

"Heating it shifts it back toward the reactants. Cooling it shifts it forward." He said it and then, because it sounded too simple, said it again with the other half attached. "The forward reaction gives off heat. So when I add heat, the system runs in reverse, like it's absorbing what I put in."

"So your project is better now than it was this morning," Spencer said, mouth full. "You found something out. Isn't that the whole thing?"

"My board says the opposite of what happens."

"Then fix the board."

Charles looked down the row. Two tables over, a girl with a seismograph made of springs was recalibrating something with a screwdriver, unbothered, as though being wrong in public were a normal Tuesday. He thought of his mother in March, telling the surgeon she'd rather know the whole result than a comfortable half of it. She'd said it lightly, holding the pamphlet, but she'd meant it, and he'd understood her better for it.

He borrowed Spencer's marker, the wide black one, and drew a single line through the word "will" on his board. Above it, in smaller print, he wrote: "predicted, incorrectly." Then, below the whole sentence: "observed result: heat shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants; the forward reaction is exothermic." His handwriting got cramped at the end, and the word exothermic ran slightly off the edge of the board, and he left it there because there was no room to redo it.

The judges came at 3:10, two of them, a man with a clipboard and a woman who introduced herself as a retired metallurgist. The man asked him to run the demonstration, so Charles switched the coil on and let the thermometer climb while they watched the blue fade, molecule by molecule it seemed, into pink. He narrated what he had expected and what he'd measured instead, and he pointed at the struck-through line on the board, and the woman leaned in to read it.

"So you got it wrong and then you found out," she said.

"Yes," Charles said, and then, because it was true, "and I still can't tell you why the forward direction is the one that gives off heat. That part I have to take on faith for now." She wrote something on her clipboard that he couldn't see. The flask sat between them, pink and warm, already shifting faintly violet at the bottom where the coil had begun to cool.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and carpet glue, and Rose's voice came back at her off the bare walls when she said "hello" to nobody. Her mother had left that morning for the closing paperwork, three towns over, and the movers were not due until Thursday, so Rose had the whole empty place to herself: a kitchen with no table, a living room with one cardboard box marked BOOKS, DO NOT CRUSH, and a phone battery at nine percent. She sat on the box because there was nothing else to sit on, and turned on the radio app to hear a human voice, any human voice, before the silence ionized the air into something that felt permanent, like the quiet had charged the whole room and would keep her suspended in it forever.

The voice belonged to a news anchor, who said that in May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy had issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States. Rose played it back twice. An epidemic. She had thought epidemics needed fevers, or at least sneezing, but apparently you could catch emptiness too, and she was fairly sure she had a case of it already, sitting on a box in a town where she knew exactly no one, unless the cashier at the gas station counted, and he had called her "buddy," which she was trying not to take personally.

She opened her messages. Mckenzie had sent a photo of the cafeteria that morning, the usual table, Paris mid-laugh with a fork raised like a judge's gavel, and underneath it: we saved you a seat anyway, it's just sitting there being a seat. Rose had not answered, because what was there to say that would not come out either sappy or fake, and she had never been good at the middle ground. Mckenzie was the talker. Rose was the one Paris called reticent, usually while elbowing her, as if the elbow would shake words loose.

Her phone buzzed. Paris: "did you die in the new house. blink twice." Rose typed back, "radio says the surgeon general called loneliness an epidemic, vivek murthy, may 2023, so technically I have a diagnosis." There was a pause, three dots, then Paris calling, because Paris did not believe in texting when a call would do, and Paris's face filling the screen was the first face Rose had seen all day that was not her own in a dark window.

"An actual epidemic," Paris said. "Like with a report and everything?"

"An advisory. I listened twice, I was taking notes in my brain." Rose held the phone up and walked it through the house, room by room, narrating like a real estate agent with a tragic portfolio. "This is where the couch will go. This is where I will eat cereal standing up for six months. This is the famous hallway where I will talk to myself." Paris laughed so hard she dropped her own phone, and Rose heard her scrambling on the floor of the cafeteria parking lot, saying wait, wait, don't hang up, my headphones are around my neck somewhere.

Then Paris turned serious in the way that made her terrible at poker. "Mckenzie thinks you're going to ghost us. She won't say it, she just keeps looking at your empty seat like it's a math problem." Rose sat down on the box again. She had been planning, in a small dishonest part of herself, to let the distance do the work, to fade out and let the friendship become a photo album, because leaving was easier if it happened to her instead of being chosen. But an epidemic, if that's what it was, did not care whether you had chosen it, and apparently neither did friends who saved a seat for nobody.

"I'm not ghosting," Rose said. "I'm just bad at this. Put Mckenzie on. No, actually, don't put her on, I'll call her tonight, seven o'clock her time, I'm putting it in the calendar with an alarm and everything. I'll be the most reliable person in her entire phone." Paris said, "You'd better be, I'm telling her you said that, and she's going to make you recite it like a poem," and Rose said, "Tell her I'll recite it standing in the famous hallway," and she lifted the phone one more time to show the bare wall where her voice would have to do until Thursday, when the boxes came and the house started being a place where somebody lived.

At seven that evening she stood in the hallway with the phone warm against her ear, and before Mckenzie even said hello, Rose heard her inhale like she'd been waiting by the phone, which, knowing Mckenzie, she had.

"Okay," Mckenzie said. "Recite it."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Five US states, Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon, have no statewide sales tax.
story:
Audrey's first paycheque opened on the screen like a riddle posed in her own name. She had worked eleven shifts at the garden centre since March, hauling petunias and ringing up mulch, and she had been imagining the number $412.50 all week, the way you imagine a door you're about to walk through. Instead the direct deposit notice said $339.18. She sat at the kitchen computer in her sock feet and read the breakdown twice, then a third time, because surely the lines would rearrange themselves if she stared hard enough. Federal income tax. State income tax. FICA, whatever FICA was, which sounded like a cat coughing. She had earned $412.50 and been handed $339.18, and nobody had asked her permission.

"Mrs. Hendricks said deductions," said her mother from the sink, not turning around. "You could ask her. Or ask the internet."

The internet was worse. The internet wanted her to know about brackets and withholding and refundable credits, and after twenty minutes Audrey felt a specific flavour of ennui, the kind that comes from discovering that adulthood was a paperwork genre all along. She texted Ember, who replied with a screenshot of her own paycheque from the ice cream stand and the message "we are being robbed, legally." That helped more than the internet.

The laptop was the thing. That was the actual want underneath all of it. Audrey's machine was six years old and made a sound like a small appliance dying whenever she opened more than three tabs, and she needed one for the graphic design course she'd been accepted into at the community college in the fall. The course welcome email had been incisive on this point: students must arrive with a machine capable of running the software. No machine, no course. She had been saving since January, and the paycheque arithmetic mattered because every dollar vacuumed away by FICA was a dollar not becoming a laptop.

Then Ember called, breathless, from the floor of her aunt's living room two towns over. "Okay, so my cousin lives in Oregon, right, and he says when he buys stuff there's no sales tax at all. None. The sticker price is the price."

"Everywhere has sales tax," Audrey said.

"Not everywhere! He says five states have no statewide sales tax. Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon. Five. He just told me, he's very smug about it."

Audrey pulled the laptop spreadsheet she'd been keeping, the one where $680 in savings met $749.99 plus the local 7 percent sales tax and fell about $121 short. She typed the five state names into a note. Her aunt lived forty minutes away, which was not Oregon. Her grandmother, however, lived in Portland. And Audrey was, in fact, expected at her grandmother's for the last week of June.

Here is where the two arguments in her head met and had it out. Argument one: her father had lambasted big-box stores her whole life for exactly this move, driving across borders to dodge the taxes that paid for the roads you drove on, and she had absorbed enough of it to feel the shape of the hypocrisy. Argument two: $121 was three and a half shifts of hauling petunias, shifts that had already been shrunk by deductions she'd never agreed to, and the state would still collect its income tax off every one of her paycheques either way. She sat with both of them. She did not resolve them into something clean, and she suspected that people who claimed they had were lying or hadn't thought about it.

The tax return, when she opened that tab, complicated her further. Apparently some of the withheld money might come back to her in the spring, because she'd earned so little that year, and there was a form for it, and the form was free, and a website walked her through it in language that was almost human. She filed it at the kitchen table on a Tuesday, mostly out of spite, and felt a small and ridiculous triumph when the confirmation screen said accepted.

"Grandma," she said on the phone that night, "is there a computer store near you? A real one, with prices taped to the shelves?"

"There's one on Hawthorne. Why, what are you plotting?"

"Nothing. Bringing you the good jam. Also possibly conducting commerce." She was still not sure the Oregon plan was right rather than merely available. She had decided she could hold that open question in one hand and a debit card in the other, which struck her as the most honest arrangement available. Her father could lambaste her over dinner in July if he wanted; she would have the laptop by then either way.

"Bring the apricot," her grandmother said. "And don't let them sell you the extended warranty. That's the real tax."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
Gabriel arrived at the food bank at ten minutes to nine with a plastic bag of his mother's old winter gloves, because he hadn't known what else to bring, and a form folded into quarters in his back pocket. The form had a grid on it for hours and a line at the bottom for a supervisor's signature, and the grid was mostly empty, six squares filled out of the forty he needed, and the diploma ceremony was in three weeks. He had assumed, all through grade nine and most of grade ten, that volunteering was something other people did, people with patience or siblings to drive them somewhere. Now the empty squares had begun to look like a door that only opened on a schedule.

Mr. Park, who ran the place, took the gloves without comment and pointed Gabriel toward the sorting table, where a girl from his law class named Kinsley was already weighing macaroni on a kitchen scale. "You're the ten o'clock," Mr. Park said, checking a clipboard. "Or you're early. Either way, wash your hands and start on that bin."

Kinsley looked up. "You here for hours too?"

"I need thirty-four by the end of June," Gabriel said. He said it lightly, the way you'd admit you hadn't started an essay, but the number came out heavier than he intended.

"Thirty-four." She set a box of pasta on the scale and wrote the weight on a sticker. "Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma. Everybody acts like it's a secret until spring of grade twelve." She tore the sticker off and smoothed it onto the box. "I did mine spread out. Like a tax I paid a little at a time. Dana did hers all in one summer at a camp, which she says was either the best or worst month of her life, she won't commit to which."

Gabriel started pulling dented cans from the bin, checking the seals the way Mr. Park had shown a previous volunteer, whose hands he'd watched through the window of the washroom door. "I thought it was twenty," he admitted. "I've been telling people it was twenty since grade nine."

"That's not a colloquialism, that's just wrong." Kinsley smiled so he'd know it wasn't cruel. "Twenty's what my uncle says, but he went to school in Ohio. Different country, different number."

The morning organized itself around them. A delivery arrived at ten, pallets of yogurt with two weeks left before the best-before date, and Gabriel learned that food banks take those dates as suggestions rather than laws, and that a pallet jack turns on a circle no wider than a dinner plate. He learned that clients, which was the word Mr. Park used, were given points rather than money, and that the points were a kind of currency you couldn't monetize or save or trade, only spend, once a week, on shelves that changed with whatever the grocery stores couldn't sell. Gabriel found himself wondering how a system like that got built, whether someone had sat in this same room and invented it out of nothing, or whether it had accreted, the way school rules did, one patch on the last.

A man came in at eleven with a rolling suitcase and a boy of about seven, and the boy wanted the yogurt with the cartoon on it, and the man said, quietly, not sadly, just factually, "We get what we get," and the boy accepted this with a shrug that struck Gabriel as more grown than anything Gabriel had done that year. Gabriel restocked the shelf so the cartoon yogurt was at the boy's eye level, not the top, and the boy took two, and the man looked at Gabriel for half a second longer than a stranger would, and Gabriel felt something shift in him that he did not have a word for.

Kinsley had watched the whole thing while pretending to weigh lentils. "See, that's the part nobody tells you," she said. "The hours are the reason you come. They're not the reason you stay."

"That feels like a thing people say."

"It is a thing people say. It's also true. Both can be true." She weighed the lentils. "Dana says I get lugubrious about the food bank. Like I'm composing a eulogy for dented cans. She's probably right."

Gabriel worked through the lunch rush and then, when Mr. Park asked if he could stay past two, looked at the form in his pocket and found he'd stopped calculating. He could do the arithmetic easily, seven Saturdays at the outside, but the arithmetic had gone quiet, the way a clock does when you stop hearing it. He wasn't sure the feeling would last. It might be a morning's feeling, specific to cartoon yogurt and a boy's shrug, and by Tuesday he might be back to counting squares. He decided that uncertainty was allowed. He could hold both things: the requirement, which was real and closing in, and whatever this was, which was also real and didn't fit in a grid.

"I can stay till five," he said.

Mr. Park initialed the form without ceremony and handed it back. "Sign the sheet by the door when you leave. And Gabriel." He was already turning toward the cooler. "Same time next Saturday?"

"Two Saturdays," Gabriel said. "Maybe three."

Kinsley, from the sorting table, held up a can of beets with a dent like a thumbprint. "Last one," she called. "You get the good jobs when you stay late."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, the usual North American graduation processional, premiered in 1901 in Liverpool.
story:
The line outside the gymnasium doors moved at a glacial pace, and Dylan, wedged between Kobe and a boy from his chemistry class, found himself humming the tune the band had been cycling for twenty minutes, the one that rolled forward and upward and never seemed to arrive anywhere. "What even is that song," he said, not quite a question. Kobe shrugged inside his rented gown. "Graduation music. It's like law." Amelya, ahead of them, turned around with her cap tilted back and said her cousin had walked to it in Edmonton and her mother had walked to it in Manila, which seemed strange to Dylan, that one melody could be rented out to so many different lives.

They walked, eventually, to that same melody, across a floor chalked with tape marks, and Dylan shook the principal's hand and received a folder with his name printed on a sticker, and then it was over in the way large things are over, all at once and slightly before you are ready.

The restaurant Ms. Foster had chosen for the dinner was narrow and warm, with exposed brick and a kitchen door that swung open on a breath of garlic whenever a waiter passed through. Ms. Foster had been Dylan's English teacher for two years and had invited a handful of students she called her "stubborn cases," which was, everyone agreed, a compliment. She wanted them to have one last table together before the summer scattered them, and she had already ordered the bread.

Kobe's want announced itself before the menus did. His father had arranged a job for him at the insurance office where his brother worked, filing and answering phones, and Kobe kept calling it what it was, a sinecure, a seat with nothing expected of it, and he kept saying it in the tone of a man trying to talk himself out of something. "Nine weeks," he said, tearing the bread. "I could save four thousand dollars. Or I could go with Amelya's brother and deck houses all summer and actually learn something." Amelya said the deck work paid worse and destroyed your hands, and Kobe said he knew, and took more bread.

When the waiter came, Dylan ordered the short rib, and Amelya ordered the same thing, and Kobe ordered the trout because Ms. Foster recommended it, and then Amelya, who had been thumbing her phone since the bread arrived, set it face up on the table between the water glasses. "Okay," she said. "I looked it up. That song. It's Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March Number One, and it premiered in 1901 in Liverpool." She said it flatly, the way she delivered everything she considered unarguable. "Liverpool," Kobe repeated, as if the city itself were the strange part.

Dylan turned his water glass a quarter turn and thought of his grandfather, who had died in March, in the winter of Dylan's senior year. There had been a service at the funeral home and, at the end of it, a recording of bagpipes, because his grandfather had liked bagpipes, and Dylan's mother had gripped his sleeve and whispered that her father had once marched to Elgar in a schoolyard in Glasgow, sixty-some years ago, a boy in a borrowed blazer, and that she hadn't known that about him until an aunt mentioned it at the wake. Dylan had held that fact for months without a shelf to put it on. Now he set it beside Amelya's phone: a melody written in 1901 in Liverpool, crossing an ocean, landing in a Scottish schoolyard, then a gymnasium in a town nobody had heard of, then him, humming it in a rented gown without knowing its name. The tune had outlasted everyone it had carried, and would carry more after him, and somehow that was not sad but steadying, the way a handrail is steadying.

"That's what I was humming," he said. "At the doors. I couldn't place it." Amelya nodded, already scrolling on. Kobe leaned over to look at her screen and said, "So every person who ever graduated here got the same entrance music as some kid in Liverpool a hundred years ago," and Dylan said, "And my grandpa. In Glasgow." Ms. Foster, who had been quiet through this, listening with her chin on her hand, said only, "Traditions are long loans," and then flagged the waiter for another bottle of sparkling water, because Kobe had emptied the first one himself.

The food came, and the conversation turned to dorms and orientations and whether Kobe should take the office job. Dylan found himself arguing both sides without meaning to: that four thousand dollars was four thousand dollars, and that a summer spent learning nothing in a chair was a kind of debt too, one you paid later in restlessness. He said it and heard how unsure it sounded, and he let it stand. Kobe said he'd decide by Friday. Amelya said that was what he'd said about prom, and Kobe said nothing, and ate his trout.

Outside, after, the parking lot was half empty and smelled of rain that hadn't started yet. Ms. Foster hugged each of them and told them to write actual letters, which nobody promised. Kobe's older brother pulled up in the truck, and Kobe stood with his hand on the door, keys to the insurance office already in his fist where his father had put them that morning. He looked at Dylan across the lot, shrugged, and got in. Amelya was still at the table inside, signing the receipt, her phone glowing beside the wine list, and through the restaurant window Dylan could hear the kitchen radio faintly, some other song entirely, going out to the dishwasher who was singing along.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
Felix refreshed the page even though the portal said decisions would post at five o'clock and it was barely noon. The bar at the top of the screen still read "Application Complete," which had stopped feeling like reassurance weeks ago and now felt more like a door held shut from the other side. Behind him the kitchen smelled like his mother's lunch, rice going cold while she worked her second job from the phone in the hallway. He had applied to six colleges, and he had chosen them with a spreadsheet his father never saw, columns for tuition, average aid, and a final column labeled only with a question mark.

Josephine had built the same spreadsheet, which was why she was on his screen now, video call squared into the corner. "Did you check the aid policies?" she asked. She was eating cereal at her own desk three miles away, a connoisseur of application deadlines who could recite which school wanted which essay supplement on two hours of sleep. "Because I found something on the Hollis website. They say right there they're need-aware."

"What does that mean?" Tiger cut in from the third window, audio only, since his camera had broken in October and he refused to replace it. Felix heard him typing anyway, the way he typed during everything, as though conversation were something to be transcribed.

"Need-blind admission means a college decides who to admit without looking at whether you can pay," Josephine said, milk-spoon clicking. "Hollis isn't. A lot of places aren't. They're need-aware instead, so if you need a lot of aid, that can count against you." She let it sit a second. "Both of us need a lot of aid."

Felix looked at his own spreadsheet and felt the question mark column go hot in his face. He had ranked his schools by reputation and by the gut feeling he got from their websites, which was, he understood now, a visceral kind of stupidity, the sort that felt like intuition. He had put Hollis second. He had put Wexford, his reach, first, and he had never once scrolled to the financial aid page, because his father had said the money would work itself out, and Felix had wanted that to be true badly enough to not check.

He checked now. Wexford's aid page took four clicks to reach and used the phrase "need-blind for domestic applicants" in a paragraph near the bottom. He read it twice, then opened Hollis and found the blunter language Josephine had found, the word "need-aware" sitting in a FAQ like a warning label on something already swallowed. Tiger was quiet on the line, then said, "So the schools where we can't pay are the schools that might not want us because we can't pay." Nobody corrected him.

Ms. Kim, who had agreed to write his recommendation and who lived two floors down, knocked at four with a plate of leftover kimbap because, she said, his mother had mentioned he wasn't eating much this week. He let her in because refusing Ms. Kim was like refusing weather. She saw the spreadsheet over his shoulder, saw the question mark column, and said nothing about his father's promise or his mother's phone calls. She only said, "You have an hour. What would you do with it?" which was the kind of question she asked instead of advice, and which he resented and followed anyway.

He spent the hour rebuilding the columns. He ranked the schools a second time, this time by what they said about need, and the list reordered itself so thoroughly that Hollis dropped to fifth and a school he'd applied to as an afterthought, Crestline, rose near the top, plain and unfamous and need-blind. He thought about his father, whose plan was that Felix would indemnify the whole family against the bad years by becoming the first one through the gate, whatever the gate cost. He thought about Josephine, who had read the fine print before the fine print could read her. He did not know which list was more honest, the one built on wanting or the one built on arithmetic, and he wrote that in the margin of a notebook his father would also never see.

At 5:04 the portal changed. The button that had said "Application Complete" now said "View Update," and Felix's hand hovered over the mouse while Josephine stopped chewing and Tiger stopped typing for the first time all day. Ms. Kim set the plate down on the desk, closer to his elbow, where he could reach it after.

"Together," Josephine said. "On three."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
The gravel road narrowed between fence posts, and Sierra's grandmother, riding in the back seat, leaned forward against her seatbelt to say what she had said twice already: if a deer came out, pump the brakes. Mr. Yoon, in the passenger seat with his clipboard on his knee, said nothing, which Sierra had learned to read as disagreement held politely in reserve.

"Grandma learned on a pickup with no anti-lock brakes," Sierra said, mostly to the windshield. "That's what you did then. Pumped."

"Worked fine for forty years," her grandmother said.

Mr. Yoon cleared his throat. "We'll get to braking," he said, and told Sierra to check her mirror, which was his way of moving the car and the conversation both forward.

She had wanted this lesson for months, and not for the reasons Jamie assumed, which were all about freedom and late-night drives to the lake. Sierra wanted the skill the way she wanted most things: quietly, thoroughly, on her own schedule. She was, her mother liked to say, an autodidact, someone who taught herself guitar from library books and chemistry from videos the summer before tenth grade. But driving resisted that. Driving required a car, a road, and another human being sitting beside her judging her following distance, and she had put it off until the summer before college because of exactly that.

The road straightened out past the Hollis farm, and Mr. Yoon had her do three controlled stops, easy ones, foot easing down until the car settled like a horse told to stand. On the third one a pheasant went up out of the ditch, loud as a door slamming, and her grandmother's hand found the back of Sierra's seat and gripped it. Sierra's foot pressed and held, smooth and hard, and the car stopped short and clean and she had not panicked, which she noted with a private, unshareable satisfaction.

"With anti-lock brakes," Mr. Yoon said, "in an emergency you press firmly and hold it, you don't pump. And you can still steer while you're braking." He said it lightly, the way he said everything, like he was mentioning weather. "Your grandmother's advice was right for the trucks she drove. It's out of date now."

"So I just... hold it down and steer?"

"Hold and steer. That's the whole trick."

Her grandmother made a small sound that could have been a laugh or could have been the seatbelt adjusting itself, and looked out the window at the bean field going by.

Here was the thing Sierra turned over for the next mile, her hands at ten and two while the gravel popped under the tires: she had spent her life treating knowledge as a thing you collected in layers, the new stuff stacked on top of the old, and the old stuff composting underneath into something harmless. But her grandmother's braking advice wasn't harmless compost. It was wrong in a way that could put her into a fence post, and it had been right, once, for a person she loved, in a world that had since changed under that person's hands without anyone sending a notice. Jamie would say the lesson was obvious, never trust anyone over forty. Sierra found that boring and also lazy, because Grandma's forty years of driving included the thirty-something that made her good at everything else: reading the road, knowing where deer crossed, easing off before a curve you couldn't yet see. The old knowledge and the new weren't enemies. They were, at worst, roommates who disagreed about one specific thing, and Sierra's job was to know which thing.

She could not fully amortize the cost of that insight, to use her father's word from the kitchen table, the way he talked about spreading the price of the tractor over the years it would last. How many of her own certainties were the equivalent of pumped brakes, correct for a road that had since been repaved? There was no way to inventory them in advance. You found out when the deer came out.

The deer came out at the creamery curve, a doe and then, three heartbeats behind, a second one, both of them stupid with morning. Sierra braked hard, held it, felt the pedal do something she hadn't asked for and didn't understand, and turned the wheel while the car was still slowing, and the car went where she pointed it, angling into the empty lane and then straightening, and the second deer cleared the fender by a margin she chose not to estimate.

"Good," Mr. Yoon said. He wrote something on his clipboard. "That's what the pedal doing that means, by the way. It's working."

"Anti-lock," Sierra said, mostly to herself.

In the back seat her grandmother was quiet for a long moment, and then, ebullient in the way of someone deciding to be, said, "Well. You held it and you steered. I'll be damned." She patted the seat twice, like a horse that had stood. "Turn here at the mailbox, sweetheart. The road's better on the other side of the creek."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
The morning the literary magazine proofs came back, Lily taped a note above her desk in the publications room that said be honest, be kind, and then spent most of third period staring at it, because the proofs were Heath's story, and Heath's story was a problem.

He had given her a story about a boy who finds his late grandfather's fishing boat and, in the final paragraph, the boat's name turns out to be the boy's own name, and there is crying. Lily had read it twice on the bus, the second time with a pencil, and the margins filled up with things she could not say out loud. The dialogue was stiff. The reveal relied on coincidence. And yet the middle, the part where the boy sands the hull alone, was so good that she had put her hand flat against the page.

"You're making a face," Heath said. He had come in early to help fold the proofs, even though folding was Lily's job as editor, even though the magazine had no budget and they were expected to commodify every square inch of it with ads for the orthodontist and the bagel place. "That's your face for when you hate something."

"I don't hate it."

"Then what's the face for?"

Mr. Papadopoulos, who supervised the magazine from behind a desk of unclaimed binders, looked up long enough to say "Two minutes" and point at the clock, because the printer was coming to collect the proofs at lunch. Lily understood, with a clarity that felt almost physical, that she could say the middle was lovely and the ending needed work and let the sentence do no work at all, the way she had done with Jeffery's poems all fall, and that she would be doing it again, not kindly but lazily, letting him walk around with a bad story stapled to his name.

"That study," Jeffery said, wandering in with a box of envelopes. He was always announcing studies. "The one Mr. Papadopoulos mentioned at the start of term. In 2014, David Yeager led a study where students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them." He set the box down. "I've been thinking about it since."

Heath looked at the wall. "So you're saying I'm the essay."

"I'm saying Lily's the teacher."

"It's not that simple," Lily said. "The note can't be a trick. If you say you believe in someone just to get to the hard part, they can tell. Then it's just semantics, the same insult wearing a nicer shirt."

"It's not semantics if you actually believe it," Jeffery said. "Do you?"

She did. That was the thing she had not said to anyone, not even in the margins: she believed the boat story could be good, not out of politeness but because she had read the sanding scene four times. What she didn't believe was that she could say so without the rest coming out wrong, and she was honest with herself about that uncertainty even as she pulled the marked-up proof across the desk.

"Okay. Two things, Heath." She put her finger on the middle section. "This part, the sanding, I've read it four times. It's the best thing in the magazine this issue. The details do the feeling for you, the grit in the seams, the radio he can't fix. You don't tell me once what to feel and I felt everything." She watched his shoulders come down maybe a centimeter. Then she turned the page. "The ending undoes it. The boat having his name is a coincidence doing your job for you, and the crying in the last line tells me how to feel when the sanding scene never did. I think you know it. I think you wrote the crying because you didn't trust the middle, and you should."

The clock gave them ninety seconds. Heath was quiet, his thumb running along the fold of the proof, and Lily realized she was holding her breath, not because she feared his anger, she had seen his vitriolic reviews of the school play and survived, but because she had put the middle of herself on that desk next to the middle of his story.

"Print the issue," Heath said finally. "Give me the weekend. If I can't fix the ending by Monday, run it as is and I'll live with it." He picked up the pencil she had left on the page, turned to the last paragraph, and drew one line through it, all the way across, then looked up at her. "Four times, really?"

The printer's van was in the lot already. Lily carried the proofs to the door, the stack lighter than she expected, and when she turned back, Heath was still at the desk, writing something in the margin where the crying had been.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
At the table, Charlie set down her fork and said, "I have a lemma."

"Is that contagious?" her father asked, reaching for the bread anyway.

"A minor theorem," Charlie said. "A small thing you prove on the way to a bigger thing. Myles says it about everything. It's contagious that way."

The kitchen smelled of burnt garlic, which her mother refused to acknowledge, stirring the pot with the composure of a woman who believed that if she never mentioned it, the char would not exist. Charlie's brother was stacking green beans into a tower. It was that kind of dinner, the kind where nobody was going anywhere, which was exactly the problem, because Charlie needed to go somewhere, or at least she needed to figure something out before Monday.

"Myles flopped his solo at Saturday's game," she said. "Second time. He keeps dropping the ball right at the cut, and I said nothing. Again."

Her mother set the pot down. "You said nothing because you're kind."

"I said nothing because I'm a coward with good branding." Charlie pulled her phone from her pocket, thumbed through it, and found the screenshot she'd taken in the library that afternoon. "Ms. Leung had this book out on the shelf, and I stole an hour with it between classes. Radical Candor. Kim Scott, 2017." She turned the screen so her brother could see, though he was mainly interested in the green bean tower's structural integrity. "Scott says good feedback is two things at once. You care personally about the person, and you challenge them directly. Not one or the other. Both."

Her father leaned back. "So the trick is?"

"The trick is I've been doing neither, or half of one. I care about Myles, so I don't challenge him, and then he keeps dropping the ball and the whole relay suffers, and by Sunday he's miserable anyway. Silent isn't kind. Silent is just quiet."

"That sounds suspiciously like a lemma," her brother said.

"It's worse. It's a whole theorem and I still have to run the proof on Monday." Charlie put the phone face down next to her plate, which in her family was the gesture of a person committing to something. "Here's my problem. If I say 'Myles, you're dropping the ball,' that's true and useless. He knows. What do I actually say?"

"Say what a good coach would say," her mother offered, ladling out a soup that had gone from burnt to a kind of dark, complicated flavor that everyone would pretend was on purpose.

"A good coach would say what, specifically?" Charlie beseeched the table, both hands out, palms up, as if the answer might be passed like the bread. "Because 'nice' isn't it. Ethen tried nice last month. He said 'great effort, buddy,' and Myles gave him a look like Ethen had patted him on the head, and then Myles went florid, the full tomato, and didn't speak to him for two days. Nice with nothing inside it reads as pity. Everyone can smell the difference."

Her father, who spent his days delivering performance reviews to people who feared them, set his spoon down with interest. "So what's the thing you actually saw? Not the verdict. The thing."

Charlie opened her mouth, then closed it, which was unlike her. "He rushes the catch," she said slowly. "He looks at the defender before he's got the ball secured, every time. Like he's planning the next move before he's finished this one. I've watched it happen four times and I never told him because..." She stopped at the edge of the sentence and stepped off. "Because he's Myles. He taught me the crossover when I was eleven and terrible. It felt disloyal to notice his flaw."

"Notice is free," her father said. "The disloyalty would be letting him keep it."

"Okay." Charlie pulled her phone back and typed, reading half aloud. "Myles. Your head's on the defender before the ball's in your hands. Watch it into your grip, then look up. I'm telling you because I watch every game hoping you get the ball, and it's killing me when it goes down." She looked up. "Too much?"

"The last sentence is a bit florid for a gym," her brother said.

"That's the caring personally part," Charlie said. "That's the whole point. Challenge without it is just Ethen's 'great effort, buddy' pointing the other direction."

She rehearsed it twice more over soup, once too stiff, once so jokey that even she had to admit the note would be lost under the laughing. The third version sat somewhere in the middle, like most true things. When she'd finally settled on it, she set the phone down again and admitted the part she hadn't said out loud yet.

"I don't know if he'll take it well. Scott's book gives me the shape of it, care plus directness, but it can't tell me how Myles hears things on a Monday after a loss. That part stays mine to find out."

Her mother began clearing bowls. Her brother's tower of green beans finally collapsed with a small, dignified slide. Charlie helped stack the dishes, then went to the doorway and stood there a moment, phone in her back pocket, running the sentence one last time.

"Watch it into your grip," she said to the empty hall, and nodded once, like a girl leaving for practice.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
Ava spread the two articles across the kitchen table like cards she had been dealt rather than cards she had chosen. Both asked the same question, whether later school start times actually improved adolescent attention, and both had been photocopied by Mr. Suryanto, who taught the research seminar and had assigned a critical review due at eight the next morning. The one from the Journal of Adolescent Health Sciences sat on the left. The one from a smaller journal she had never heard of, School Hours Quarterly, sat on the right, its pages thinner, its typeface older, its argument longer and harder to follow.

She had until eight in the morning, and it was already past ten. Her mother had gone up with a mug of tea and a warning that the dishwasher needed emptying before bed, which meant Ava kept glancing at the clock and then at the dishwasher and then back at the articles, as if the three of them were competing for something.

The problem was not that she did not understand the articles. It was that she could not decide which one to trust, and Jayla and Emery, who had come over after the writing club meeting that afternoon, had made it worse. Emery had pulled up a number on her phone and set it on the table between the granola bars. "The big journal has an impact factor of eleven," Emery had said. "The little one is under two. That settles it. The first article is better."

Ava had looked at the number for a long moment. "What does impact factor even count?"

"It counts prestige," Emery said, with the flat certainty that made her sound belligerent even when she was only being sure. Ava had learned to hear the difference, mostly. "Everyone uses it."

Jayla had stacked her granola bar wrapper into a small square, which she did when she was thinking. "My cousin reviews for a physics journal," she said slowly. "She says it's a citation count. It's the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years. That's the whole thing. It's not a grade. It's an average."

Emery had waved this off. "Averages are grades."

Ava had said nothing then. She had taken the phone, thanked them, walked them to the door, and come back to the table with the feeling of a word half remembered. Now, alone, she wrote the sentence out on a legal pad, because writing things out was how she made them real; she did not want to reify a number into a verdict without checking what the number was made of. The impact factor was an average of citations. It told you, in a rough and aggregated way, how often the journal's recent articles got cited. It did not tell her whether this article, the one under her lamp, with its careful sample of nine schools and its honest list of limitations, was better than the article in the famous journal with its slicker statistics and its smaller sample of two.

She read both conclusions again. The famous journal's article claimed a large effect and buried its caveats in a footnote so dense it read like an epigram, brief and clever and impossible to argue with. The obscure journal's article claimed a modest effect, admitted it could not separate the start time change from a new bus schedule introduced the same year, and suggested, in plain sentences, exactly what further research would need to do. Ava noticed that her pencil had, without her deciding it, moved to the margins of the modest article, underlining, questioning, agreeing.

The high impact factor told her that the famous journal was cited often, which could mean its work was influential, or fashionable, or simply positioned where everyone looked first. It was an average over everything the journal published, and an average could hide a varied set the way a smooth lake hides stones. She could not prove which article was truer. She could prove, from the methods sections alone, that one of them showed her its reasoning and the other showed her its results, and she found, reading back over her notes, that she trusted the one that showed its reasoning, even knowing her trust was a judgment and not a measurement.

She wrote until one in the morning, emptied the dishwasher at one fifteen because her mother would check, and printed the review at one forty. Six pages. In the last paragraph she wrote that the citation average could not settle the comparison, that both articles deserved respect, and that the question of which claim would hold up remained, for now, genuinely open, which was not the same as her not having an opinion.

At breakfast Mr. Suryanto's email arrived before she had finished her toast. One line. "Come find me at lunch. I want to hear which one you believed, and why."

Ava slid the review into her folder, pinned her hair back with the pencil still behind her ear, and said to the empty kitchen, "The small one. But I'll argue about it."

On the way out she picked up the legal pad, the sentence about citations still sitting at the top in her own handwriting, and set it on the counter where her mother would see it.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The last two minutes of the game took eleven minutes of clock time and a penalty review, and when the receiver held on in the end zone, the living room detonated. Gavin's father was on his feet with both hands on his head, the way men do when they cannot physically contain a result. Kristian, who had never played a down of organized football in his life, stood on the couch and shouted it at the ceiling: "We won. We actually won."

Gavin stayed in the armchair with his drink sweating against his palm. He had been circumspect all afternoon about the game, mostly because he had spent the previous Thursday in the school library avoiding a history paper and reading, instead, a battered paperback about persuasion. One chapter had stuck with him. In 1976, a psychologist named Robert Cialdini had looked at students on big football campuses and found that after their team won, they wore more of the university's clothing, and that they said "we" more often when describing wins than when describing losses. Gavin had copied the detail into his notebook under a heading he now found embarrassing, which was "people are ridiculous."

The flashback that visited him, as Kristian climbed down from the couch, was not of the library. It was of October, junior year, when the team had lost in overtime and Gavin had walked home behind two older boys from his street. He remembered how they talked about it. "They couldn't stop the run," one said, and, "the quarterback threw it right to him." Not we. They. Gavin had felt superior to them at the time, cataloguing their pronouns like a little scientist, and then had gone home and worn his school hoodie to the diner anyway, the morning after a win, without ever asking himself why.

Gianna, folded into the corner of the sectional with her shoes off, noticed him not cheering. "You're doing your face," she said. "The one where you think everyone else is a lab rat."

"I'm not." He was, a little. "It's just, there was this study. Cialdini, 1976. Students wore more school stuff after their team won, and they said 'we' for wins and not for losses." He kept his voice even so it wouldn't sound like a lecture.

Kristian, still flushed, turned from the window where he'd been texting someone the score. "So you're saying I'm one of those guys."

"I'm saying everyone's one of those guys. Including me." Gavin told them about the hoodie, about the two boys in October, and it came out more like a confession than an argument, which surprised him. He had planned, in some vague way, to hold the study over Kristian's head. Instead he found himself handing it over like evidence for the defense. "The weird part is that after a loss, people push it away. Like the team did it to them. And after a win, they pull it in."

Gavin's father lowered himself back onto the sofa, wincing at his knees, and looked at his son with an expression that was not hostile but was not warm either. "You want us to say 'they won' so you can feel smart?"

"No." Gavin considered the question honestly, because that was the trap in it, and he could see the trap. "I want to figure out whether it's actually bad. Being glad because a team you didn't play for won. My uncle says it makes people feel like they're part of something bigger than themselves, and that's good for them. My psych book kind of says we're all just borrowing the glory. I don't know which one it is. Maybe both."

Gianna pulled her shoes back on, which was a gesture Gavin had learned to read as her deciding a conversation had become worth participating in properly. "My mom does it with the royal family," she said. "We when they have a wedding, they when somebody gets arrested. She's never met any of them."

Kristian sat down on the couch arm, deflating slowly. "So when I texted my cousin 'we won,' I was doing the exact thing from your study."

"You were doing the exact thing from the study," Gavin agreed. "I've done it too. I'm not trying to absolve myself by saying that, either. I did it in October and I didn't even notice."

Nobody spoke for a second. On the muted television, the highlights had already begun, the same catch replayed from a better angle, and Gavin's father reached for the remote but didn't turn the sound up. He was watching the receiver spike the ball, and Gavin watched him watch it, and thought about how his father had been saying "we" for forty years, and how it had never once seemed to cost him anything, and how Gavin could not decide whether that was a failure of attention or a kind of skill.

"Okay," Kristian said finally, standing. "Then we're getting pizza. And when I say 'we,' I mean Gianna and me, because you're the one who's going to explain the whole thing again at the door."

Gavin got his jacket off the hook by the stairs.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
story:
The food bank shared a wall with the animal shelter, and on Saturday mornings the dogs on the other side of the drywall started barking before anyone had even unlocked the folding tables. Sara had signed up because the scholarship application wanted community service, a fact she had compartmentalized so thoroughly that by the time she pushed through the door she half believed she was there for the animals. Mr. Moretti, who ran the distribution, handed her a hairnet and a crate without ceremony.

"Gleaning drop-off came in," he said. "Farmers leave crops in the fields after the main harvest, food that would just go to waste otherwise, and volunteers go out and pick it. That squash is from this morning."

So the pile of butternut squash by the loading dock had a name, and the name was the smallest thing Sara learned that day. William was already there, sorting. She hadn't known he volunteered. She hadn't known, either, that his address was two streets over from the shelter, close enough that walking here was easier than taking the bus, and she filed that away without letting herself think about why the address mattered.

The morning had a rhythm: weigh, box, stack. Mr. Moretti kept the ledger, calling out weights, and between the numbers he talked to the clients by name. Some took the squash gratefully. One man stood at the table a long time, hands in his pockets, as if accepting food required a deliberation Sara could not see the inside of. William leaned toward her and said, quietly, "He was my math teacher freshman year." The man took three squash and left without giving his name.

Around eleven, a woman came in with a clipboard and a lanyard from the county. She counted boxes. She asked Mr. Moretti for the intake sheet from the gleaning run, and Sara, stacking nearby, saw his face change in a way she would think about later. He said the sheet was in the truck. He was gone nine minutes, which was long enough for the woman to count the boxes twice and frown at the discrepancy between her number and the ledger's.

Here is what Sara told herself, and it was not entirely true: that she had seen nothing, that the nine minutes meant nothing, that the three extra cases of squash marked for the animal shelter, where volunteers blended leftover produce into the dogs' food, were a routine transfer. She was good at this, at the encapsulation of inconvenient facts into sealed containers she never opened. She had done it with the scholarship. She could do it with a missing intake sheet.

But William had seen the ledger, too. In the parking lot, while they loaded the transfer cases onto the shelter's cart, he said, "The dogs don't eat forty pounds of squash a week." Sara's first instinct was to defend Mr. Moretti, who gave food to a man too proud to give his name, who knew every client's first name, who had been doing this longer than either of them had been alive. Her second instinct was to say nothing, because William's family lived two streets over, and she had watched him all morning with a carefulness she was ashamed of, a quiet audit of whether the food bank was something he used or something he served, and she did not want him asking what she was really here for.

"He takes the surplus to the shelter," she said, which was true. "And the shelter kicks some of it back to the families who won't come in here." Which she did not know, had invented on the spot, and which William seemed to know she had invented, because he looked at her the way her mother looked at a receipt that didn't add up.

"You didn't have to sign the hours sheet twice," William said. "Once at the farm, once here. That's how I knew you were doing it for the scholarship. It's fine. Mine's due too." He pushed the cart through the shelter's side door, into the noise of the kennels, and she followed him past the runs where the dogs stood up on their hind legs to see what she was carrying.

The squash went into cold storage beside the kibble. Mr. Moretti's truck was still in the lot when they came out, and it was still there an hour later, and Sara, sweeping the floor of the food bank alone, decided she would count the boxes again next Saturday before anyone told her not to.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: German historian Alexander Demandt compiled a list of 210 different explanations that writers have offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell.
story:
Jasmine had told everyone, twice, that the essay was basically done. She had said it at lunch on Thursday with the confidence of someone who had written a thesis statement, and she had said it again on the phone to her mother, which meant it was nearly a family fact. In reality she had a paragraph and a half, and the paragraph and a half argued that Rome fell because of lead poisoning, which she had chosen mostly because it was vivid. Now it was Saturday, and she was at her grandmother's house for the weekend with her laptop and no wifi, and the essay was due Monday.

She started in her grandmother's study, the small back room where her grandfather's books still lived in the exact order he had kept them, because her grandmother would not let anyone move a single spine. Jasmine remembered the study as a place of order and certainty. She remembered her grandfather, a retired history teacher, as a man who had known exactly why everything happened. She was almost sure he had told her once that Rome fell for one clear reason. She could not remember which one, only the certainty.

"Looking for Rome?" her grandmother asked from the doorway, holding two cups of tea. Her voice had a querulous edge this morning, though her eyes were kind. "You'll find it under ancient history, obviously. He kept his certainties filed alphabetically."

There was something in that, but Jasmine took her tea and let it pass. She found the shelf, and on the third book down, a thin German volume with a paper bookmark at a page of notes in her grandfather's cramped hand. She could not read the German, but tucked into the book was a photocopy of an English review, and on the margin her grandfather had underlined a sentence twice. She read it standing up, one finger holding her place in the tea steam. The German historian Alexander Demandt had compiled a list of 210 different explanations that writers had offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell. Two hundred and ten. Her grandfather's note beside it said only, in pencil, "So much for one clear reason."

She sat down on the floor with the page and her cooling tea and felt the essay dissolve quietly, the way a sandcastle goes at the edge of the tide. If there were 210 explanations, then lead poisoning was not an answer; it was one voice in a very crowded room. She had built a paragraph on the idea that history was a lock with one key, and here was her own grandfather, whose certainty she had borrowed secondhand, telling the photocopy otherwise.

She called Albert from the kitchen phone, because Albert had wifi at home and no sense of urgency. "I need you to check something," she said. "A German historian, Demandt, and a number."

"Which number?" Albert asked. There was chewing on his end.

"Two hundred and ten. Explanations for why the Western Roman Empire fell. Tell me it's wrong."

There was a pause long enough for her grandmother to slide a biscuit across the counter toward her. "It's right," Albert said finally. "Two hundred and ten. It's famous. Sara-Maude brought it up in seminar when Mr. Kamau asked for one cause and she said, which of the two hundred and ten do you want." He laughed. "He liked it, apparently."

Jasmine expostulated at him for a full minute, about deadlines and the cruelty of a fact arriving on a Saturday, and then she thanked him and hung up and looked at her grandmother, who was pretending to read the back of a cereal box and clearly listening to everything. "Grandpa knew this," Jasmine said. "He underlined it."

"He argued about it," her grandmother said. "He'd say, the sources are partial, and the questions people ask change, so the answers change. Then he'd argue some more at dinner." She took the photocopy gently from Jasmine's hand and looked at the underlining. "He liked arguing more than he liked being right. You may not remember that part."

And Jasmine realized she did not, or she did but had filed it away, because certainty had been easier to carry home from those visits than doubt. She carried her tea back to the study, opened her laptop on the floor among the books, and deleted her second paragraph. She began again, and this time she wrote the essay as an argument between two ways of thinking: the one she had wanted history to be, a settled account with a single cause, and the one her grandfather had actually lived with, in which the past stayed plural because the evidence survived only in pieces and each generation asked it new questions. She kept the lead hypothesis in, honestly, as one explanation among the two hundred and ten, useful precisely for what it could not settle. She did not pretend she had resolved which way of thinking was better. She wrote that she was still deciding, and that the deciding felt like the actual work.

That evening her grandmother read the draft in the study with the lamp on, and when she finished she set the pages face down on her husband's shelf, between the alphabetized certainties, and said, "He would have argued with half of this."

"Which half?" Jasmine asked.

Her grandmother smiled and turned off the lamp. "Come to dinner and find out."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually do not include sales tax, which is added at the register, so the total is higher than the posted price.
story:
The laminated menu said fourteen dollars for the braised chicken, and Brooklyn had exactly fourteen dollars in her pocket, two fives and four singles folded since Tuesday, when her paycheque had landed in her account and then, like every paycheque, turned out to be smaller than the number she'd signed up for. She had learned that in the first week at the garden centre: her hourly rate multiplied by her hours produced a figure on a page she never saw, and what arrived in her account was that figure minus income tax, minus a deduction for something called CPP, minus a smaller deduction she couldn't name. Nobody had warned her, and when she'd asked the supervisor, he'd shrugged and said welcome to working life, in a tone that suggested he found her question charming rather than reasonable.

She put the menu down and caught Alyvia's eye across the table. "I'm getting the chicken," Brooklyn said. "It's fourteen."

"Fourteen," Alyvia repeated, in the flat voice she used when she already saw the problem. Alyvia had been working since the previous summer, at a bakery, and she had opinions about money the way other people had opinions about music. "You have fourteen on you?"

"Exactly fourteen. Why are you looking at me like that?"

Yasmin, who had ordered only a lemonade because she was saving for a concert, leaned her chin on her hand. "She's looking at you like that because she's about to let you find out on your own."

The waiter came, and Brooklyn ordered the chicken, and while they waited she turned her glass of water in slow circles. She remembered a girl at the garden centre, in the break room, holding a receipt from the vending machine and saying, "Three dollars? It says two seventy-five on the machine." Brooklyn had assumed the machine was broken. Now, watching Alyvia stack the sugar packets into a deliberate tower, she began to suspect the machine had been honest and the world around it wasn't.

"Out with it," Brooklyn said.

"Out with what?" Alyvia said, but she was smiling, and the smile was not unkind.

"The thing. The money thing. You're doing the face."

"Fine." Alyvia flattened the sugar tower with one finger. "Menu prices. Shelf prices. They're not the real price. At the register they add sales tax on top, so the total comes out higher than what's posted. That's how it works here. In Canada, in the States. Everywhere we've ever shopped, actually."

"That's insane," Brooklyn said. "The price should be the price."

"I agree. My position is that it's a scam designed to commodify honesty, but that's just me."

Yasmin laughed into her lemonade. Brooklyn didn't laugh. She was doing arithmetic in her head, the kind that felt like falling: fourteen plus some percentage she didn't know, maybe a dollar, maybe a dollar and a half, and then a tip, which Alyvia would insist on, and her fourteen dollars becoming, in the space of one register beep, not enough. She thought about the paycheque again, about all the quiet subtractions. It seemed to her that money was a thing that announced itself as one number and arrived as another, always smaller, and that no one considered this worth mentioning until you were already standing at the till with your singles laid out.

When the food came, the chicken was good, and Brooklyn ate slowly, and when the bill arrived in its black folder she opened it and looked for a long time. $14.00, then a line for HST, then $15.82. Alyvia slid two loonies across the table without a word, the way you'd pass someone a pencil, and Brooklyn pushed them back, and Alyvia pushed them forward again, and they held the coins between them on the tablecloth for a moment, neither gripping.

"I'll get you back," Brooklyn said.

"It's not a debt. It's a rounding error in the universe."

Mr. Bouchard, her old history teacher, was at the counter paying, and he raised his coffee cup to her on his way out. He had told them once, in the unit on the Sixties, that the country had offered draft dodgers amnesty, and that the word meant a wiping clean, a starting over, and Brooklyn thought about that now with her loonies still sitting between her and Alyvia, unresolved. She picked them up, finally, and put them in her pocket, where they sat quiescent against the folded bills.

At home that night she asked her mother about the tax return paperwork on the kitchen table, the envelopes with the little window, the line where you reported what you'd earned. Her mother said she might even get some of it back, some year, some part of the amount they'd already taken. "So they take it," Brooklyn said, "and then maybe give some back, and the menu price isn't the price."

Her mother looked up and said, "Now you understand," but Brooklyn wasn't sure she understood anything yet. She took out her phone and typed "sales tax rate" into the search bar.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Chicago style offers two citation systems: notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities, and author-date, common in the sciences.
story:
Alexis would have said she was not avoiding the paper, merely rotating around it, the way a planet keeps a careful distance from the thing it orbits. She had chosen her topic in September, gathered nine sources by October, and now, in November, she was sitting in the school library with all of them stacked beside her in a geological column, the newest on top like fresh igneous rock laid down over everything she had failed to write. Ms. Ramírez had returned her draft on Monday with a red circle around the first page and a single comment in the margin, and Alexis had carried that page around for three days before opening it again in the library's back corner, where the carpet was worn pale and nobody came before fourth period.

The comment read: "You've mixed systems. Chicago notes and bibliography for a history paper. See me." That was the whole letter, more or less, though Alexis reread it as if a longer message were hiding between the words. She had done the citations in a style she'd found online, parentheses in the text with the author's name and year, because that was what her chemistry lab report had used and it had looked efficient, professional even. She had assumed citation was citation, a toll one paid at the end, uniform everywhere, and she had told herself this assumption was reasonable rather than convenient.

Abbygail dropped into the chair across from her with a granola bar and no apology. "You look like your draft came back bleeding."

"It came back circled," Alexis said. "Red circle, one comment. Mixed systems."

"What does that even mean? Like you cited wrong?"

"I cited," Alexis said, with more dignity than the stack of unread sources supported. "I cited in the wrong kind of Chicago, apparently. There's more than one kind. She wrote notes and bibliography like I should know what that is."

Abbygail peeled the wrapper down. "So look it up. Isn't that the whole point of a library?"

Alexis had a private theory that looking things up was what other people did, people who hadn't already spent a month being sure. But she pulled the style manual from the reference shelf anyway, the thick blue one she'd walked past a hundred times, and found the Chicago chapter, and read it standing up with one hip against the shelf. Chicago style offered two citation systems, the manual said plainly. There was notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities. And there was author-date, common in the sciences. She read it twice. The parentheses from her chemistry lab, the name and the year: that was author-date, and it belonged to the sciences, not to a paper on the Homestead Strike. What belonged to her paper were footnotes at the bottom of the page and a bibliography at the end, which was, she realized with a small deflation, a different shape of honesty, not a toll but a trail.

She sat back down and began converting. The first footnote took her eleven minutes. The second took four. Somewhere around the sixth, Elia appeared, smelling of the gym, and leaned over her shoulder.

"Is that what you've been doing all period? Footnotes?"

"Notes and bibliography," Alexis said. "That's the system. For history. The other one's author-date, for the sciences." She said it the way one repeats a thing recently learned, testing whether it fit the mouth.

Elia squinted at the page. "It looks like the old books. Little numbers, then the little numbers again at the bottom."

"That's the point," Alexis said, and then hesitated, because she wasn't entirely sure what the point was, only that the trail now led somewhere a reader could follow. She was honest enough with herself to admit the uncertainty, sitting there with the manual open: she could perform the system without fully understanding why the humanities preferred one trail and the sciences another, and she supposed she'd find out, or she wouldn't.
