Ms. Ramírez came through at the end of the period to return a bundle of atlases, and paused at their table long enough to see the footnotes marching down the page. "Better," she said. "The argument still wanders in paragraph three, but the apparatus is honest now." She tapped the bibliography. "Alphabetical, and the titles in italics. Come Thursday if paragraph three keeps wandering." Then she was gone toward the front desk, unhurried, the way she did everything.

After school Alexis stayed until the light through the tall windows went from white to amber. She was not, she had finally decided, a person who avoided the paper; she was a person who had wanted the paper to be easy and had been slow to forgive it for not being so. She wrote two new sentences for paragraph three, deleted one, kept the other. She spread the nine sources around her like a small city and decided which buildings belonged on the map. The library emptied by degrees, the milieu thinning from a murmur to a hum to the click of the clock above the biography section. When the librarian began shutting down the computers, Alexis packed the blue manual last, and on her way out she stopped at the desk.

"Can I take this home?" she asked. "Just overnight. I'll bring it back before first period."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.
story:
The deadline was in eleven days, and William had taped the requirements sheet above his desk at school: ten artworks, one theme, and an artist's statement. He had the ten works, more or less, spread across Mr. Aydın's classroom during every free period. What he did not have was the statement, because every draft he wrote sounded like someone else describing him.

"The artist is interested in decay," he read aloud to Summer, who was eating sunflower seeds on the radiator cover and spitting the shells into her palm. "The artist uses found materials. The artist believes the city forgets its own edges."

"You sound like a museum plaque," Summer said. She tipped the shells into the trash can from three feet away and missed. "Also, why is the artist interested in decay? Are you interested in decay?"

He was, actually. He had photographed the flooded lot behind the gas station for two months, watched the rust bloom on the abandoned bikes there, glued some of that rust onto canvas with glue he'd stolen from his father's workbench. But when he wrote it down, he retreated behind the third person like a witness who didn't want to be called to testify.

Cyrus had a different theory, offered while the three of them scraped palettes in the sink after class. "It's a strategy," Cyrus said. "You write like an institution so they grade you like an institution. Very revisionist of you, actually. Undermining the whole idea of the artist from inside the artist's statement."

"That's not what I'm doing," William said, though privately he thought it was a little bit what he was doing.

Mr. Aydyn kept a shelf of catalogues at the back of the room, and William had taken to reading them during lunch, partly for ideas and partly because the room was warm and the cafeteria was not. He noticed something in a monograph about a sculptor who worked only with rope: at the front, before the essays by curators, there was a page in different type. It explained which knots she used and why, where she had learned them from her grandfather, what the harbor of her childhood town had looked like before the ferry line closed. It said I. I chose the knot because. I return every summer to. The curators' essays afterward said the artist does this, the artist intends that, but this one page was hers, in her own voice.

William read it twice, then pulled his crumpled draft from his pocket and smoothed it against the catalogue's cover. The distinction wasn't decoration. The whole point of the statement was that it was written by the artist, in the first person, explaining the ideas, the methods, the context. It was the one part of the portfolio where you were allowed to say I, maybe the only part where you had to. The essays could interpret him all they wanted; this page was where he explained himself.

He wrote a new draft that night at the long table by the window, working with an almost ascetic discipline, phone in his bag, one lamp, no music. "I photograph the flooded lot on Delmore Street because it is two blocks from my house and nobody else looks at it," he wrote. "I use rust I collect there because the materials should come from the place itself. I started in February, when the ice made everything look permanent, and kept going after it melted, because I wanted to see whether ruin changes speed when you watch it." The sentences were plainer than anything he had written before, and he kept almost revising them into fancier ones, and kept stopping himself.

The next day he gave it to Summer, who read it with the seeds still in her cheek. "It's you," she said. "Like, actually you. It's kind of unsettling."

"Is it good, though?"

"That's a different question." She handed it back, and he stood there weighing it, honest with himself about what he still didn't know: whether saying I made the work more true or only more exposed, whether the grader would read plainness as confidence or as not trying. He could feel both possibilities at once, and he couldn't yet tell which one he believed.

He brought the draft to Mr. Aydyn's desk after the bell. Mr. Aydyn read it without expression, then looked up over his glasses. "The ten pieces," he said. "The Delmore lot, all of them?"

"Eight of them. Two are the bikes from the same lot, closer up."

"Then say so. Make the statement account for all ten." He set the page down and turned to the next student's portfolio, already elsewhere.

William walked back to his seat reading the draft over, pencil behind his ear. Near the window Cyrus was arranging his own ten pieces into a grid on the floor, and outside, three floors down, the flooded lot was catching the late light, orange on the brown water. William sat down beside his photographs, spread them out in the same order as the statement, and began to write, at the top of a clean page, I.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, a field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class.
story:
Rebecca had promised herself she would finish the assignment before midnight, and it was already eleven, and the assignment was still a blank file glowing on Tayla's laptop in the basement, between a deflated air mattress and a vending machine Tayla's dad had won in a raffle and never plugged in. The task was small and supposedly simple: build a class in Java, a BankAccount with a balance, and then write a test for it. Rebecca had typed the class in nine minutes. The test was what refused to live.

"Read it out loud," Tayla said from the couch, where she was lying with her legs over the armrest, eating dry cereal out of the box like a horse. "That's what my mom does with my little brother's spelling words. It's humiliating but it works."

"It says," Rebecca said, "cannot read field balance, it has private access." She turned the laptop so Tayla could see the red underline, as if the underline might be embarrassed and retract itself.

"Maybe the computer's just capricious today," Tayla said. "Mine does that. Deletes whole essays out of spite."

"It's not spite. It's something I did." Rebecca scrolled up to the class she'd written, the one she'd been so pleased with. She'd typed the word private in front of the balance field because the worksheet said to, the way you sign a form without reading it. She looked at the word for a while. Somewhere upstairs, Tayla's dad's TV murmured through the floor.

"What," Tayla said, not a real question, just noticing that Rebecca had gone quiet in a way that usually preceded either a breakthrough or a thrown pen.

"Private," Rebecca said slowly. "I marked the balance private. And the test isn't inside the class. The test is a different file. So it can't touch it." She said it out loud and felt the sentence click into place like a seatbelt. "A field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class. That's the whole rule. That's why it won't compile."

"So un-private it."

"The worksheet says it has to stay private. Ms. Farah wants it that way."

"Then you're stuck being stoic about it," Tayla said, and crunched ostentatiously. "Very dignified. Very doomed."

Rebecca was already typing, though, because an idea had arrived the way ideas do, mid-sentence, without knocking. If the test couldn't reach the field from outside, then the field had to be reached from inside, and the class itself could offer something outward, a small public door. She wrote a method called getBalance that did nothing but hand the value back. It felt almost too easy, like leaving a note for the mail carrier instead of standing at the mailbox all day. She called the method in the test. The red underline vanished. The test ran, printed 100.0, and passed.

"Wait." Tayla sat up, cereal box abandoned, which for Tayla was the equivalent of standing ovation. "You fixed it with a method? You fixed it by adding more code?"

"That's the joke, isn't it," Rebecca said. "You lock the door and then you install a mail slot." She ran the test again just to watch the green check appear twice, because once felt like luck and twice felt like a pattern.

Mathieu came down the stairs then, back from wherever he'd been, carrying three cans of pop as if returning from an expedition. He read the screen over her shoulder with the entitlement of someone who had contributed nothing. "You used a getter," he said. "Farah's going to be pleased. She spent twenty minutes Thursday on exactly this."

"She never mentioned getters," Rebecca said.

"She mentioned them. You were drawing on your arm."

Rebecca looked at her forearm, where a faint pen vine was still visible, and decided not to extenuate the drawing, since the drawing had no defense. "Fine. But I still found it myself. She can be pleased about that too." She thought about Ms. Farah's worksheet, which had seemed arbitrary and slightly cruel at eleven o'clock, and about the green check now, and she couldn't fully decide whether the rule was a wall or a handrail. Probably it was both, which was a thing she suspected about a lot of rules, and which she was not going to say out loud in this basement.

"So what does the getter actually get you," Mathieu said, cracking a can, "besides the number?"

"Nothing, yet. Later, supposedly, I could put checks inside the class. Like, nobody withdraws a negative amount. But right now it's just a door with nobody standing behind it."

"That's the saddest thing you've ever said about code," Tayla said, and reached for a can.

Rebecca saved the file twice, once with the shortcut and once through the menu, because after a night like this she trusted nothing, then closed the laptop halfway, the way you leave a door ajar for a cat. "I'm going to write the second test at home," she said. "The withdraw one."

"With your little vine arm," Mathieu said.

"With my vine arm," Rebecca agreed. Tayla raised her can, pop sloshing faintly, and said, "To the mail slot."

fact: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995; its lead designer was James Gosling.
story:
The public library on Marsh Street kept its computer lab in the back corner, behind the periodicals, where the afternoon light came through a diaphanous curtain and softened the glare on the monitors. Victoria took the seat nearest the window because it was the only one where she could prop her notebook against the keyboard. She had three weeks before the placement test for the college's introductory programming course, and she had promised herself she would not walk into that room knowing nothing.

The book she had chosen, a secondhand copy with a cracked spine, had reached the chapter on classes. She read the rule twice: fields should be private, and access to them should come through methods the class itself provides. Getters, the book called them. She had watched her older cousin's code once, a sprawl of numbers anyone could reach in and change, and the whole program had broken because one value got altered somewhere no one remembered. There was a philosophy buried in this, she thought, something about doors and who holds the keys, and she was not sure yet whether she believed it or whether it was just a habit the language had decided for her.

Francis arrived twenty minutes late, which for Francis counted as early. He dropped into the chair beside her and opened a bag of sunflower seeds he was not supposed to have in the library. He wanted the same test passed, but he wanted it differently; he had told her last week that if he could just get the certificate, his uncle would take him seriously about the summer internship at the repair shop, and that mattered more to him than any language did. "What are they making you do," he said, cracking a seed with his back teeth.

"Build a class," Victoria said. "Book. It has to have private fields, and then getter methods to read them. And a tester that proves it works." She turned her notebook toward him. She had written the fields first, title and author and pages, then a constructor, then the small public methods that handed the values back. Below that, a tester class that made one Book and printed what the getters returned.

Francis leaned in, squinting. "Why not just make the fields public and skip all the typing?"

"That's what I asked myself," Victoria said. "But the book says the point is that the class decides what gets out. Everything has to pass through a door it built." She paused. "I half think it's about trust. You trust the object to guard its own information." She did not say the other half, which was that it might just be ceremony, a formality older people in the field had agreed to perform. She held both ideas and did not try to force them together.

Ms. Patel came by with a cart of returns and stopped, because she always stopped, and because the lab was hers to keep orderly. She had a way of reading a screen from two steps away that felt like being marked. "Are you on the Java book?" she said. "The one with the orange cover. Someone left a bookmark in chapter four." She slid it out of the cart and set it beside Victoria's elbow. "You know it goes back before you do," she added, and moved on toward the reference desk, where a man was waiting to argue about a fine.

Victoria opened the discarded copy and found the bookmark at a page of history rather than code. She read it to herself first, then aloud, because Francis had stopped chewing. "Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995," she read. "Its lead designer was James Gosling."

"Nineteen ninety-five," Francis said. He sat back. "That's older than us. By a lot. I thought this stuff was new." He looked at the screen as if the language might have aged visibly, like the curtain, like the carpet. "Somebody at the robotics meet last spring said the same thing about their code, and I didn't believe them."

Victoria typed a few lines, then stopped. She had been thinking of the private fields as a modern idea, a recent tightening, but the rule was as old as the language itself, older than either of them, decided before they could have an opinion about it. That did not settle her question of whether it was wisdom or ceremony, but it changed something; the people who built it had lived with the consequences for decades, and the book in front of her was an inheritance rather than a decree. She could take the door and the keys seriously without pretending she knew the whole reason for them. That was as far as she got, and she let it be that far.

She wrote the tester then, a small main method that created a Book and printed each getter's result, and she ran it. The first attempt failed on a missing semicolon, a red line she found and removed, and the second run printed the title, the author, and the page count in clean black text on the console. Francis copied her structure in his own file, changing only the names, and when his ran too he knocked the table lightly with his knuckle, once, the way people do when a machine starts.

The lab emptied toward dinner. Ms. Patel began switching off the far monitors, giving each terminal its nightly reprieve, and the curtain moved in the vent's slow breath. Victoria saved her file twice, then a third time, and closed the laptop over the warm keys. "Same time Thursday," Francis said, folding his seeds into his pocket. She said yes, and carried the orange book to the desk to have it checked out under her own card.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: An intersect overlay in GIS keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers, so intersecting housing with a flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone.
story:
The laptop slid across the seat with every curve in the road, and Jade caught it by the corner for the fourth time. "Can you slow down on the corners?" she said. "Half my city is about to end up in the floorwell." Mr. Bekele eased off the accelerator without answering, which Jade had learned was his way of saying yes. They were three hours out from the conference where she was supposed to present her flood map, and the map was still wrong.

She opened the file again, hoping the drive had somehow fixed it. It hadn't. Her overlay, the one she had titled "Housing at Risk of Flooding," showed every parcel in the city, all forty thousand of them, shaded in the same anxious orange whether they sat on the riverbank or on the hilltops. She had spent last night selecting, exporting, re-importing, and the result was a map of everything, which meant a map of nothing.

Jay leaned over from the middle seat, chewing the last of an epicurean stash of dark chocolate he had bought at a gas station and refused to share until now. "You look like your grandmother died," he said, offering her a square.

"My grandmother is fine. My map isn't." She turned the screen toward him. "See? It should only show the houses in the flood zone. Instead it shows the whole city."

Jay squinted. He was the one who had taught himself three scripting languages over summer and read biographies of dead polymaths for fun, which Jade found both admirable and slightly unbearable. "What tool did you use to combine them?"

"The overlay thing. I put the housing layer on top of the flood zone layer."

"That's probably union," he said. "Union keeps everything from both layers. What you want is intersect. An intersect overlay keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers." He gesticulated at the windshield as he said it, nearly knocking the chocolate into the cupholder, his hands drawing two shapes merging into one smaller shape in the air. "So intersecting housing with the flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone. Nothing else survives."

Jade stared at the screen. The whole night came back to her, the dropdown menu she had clicked through without reading, the two tools sitting side by side, union and intersect, and she had picked the first one because it was first. She deleted the layer, found intersect, and ran it. The progress bar crawled while the highway hummed. Then the map redrew itself, and the orange shrank to a narrow band along the river, dense in the east end where the older duplexes stood, thinning out where the lots got big and the houses new.

"There," Jay said.

But Jade was already zooming in, and her stomach tightened the way it did when an answer was correct and unwelcome at once. The east end cluster sat squarely on top of the neighborhood where her aunt had lived until the spring the water came up to the porch steps. Her first map, the wrong one, had let her believe the risk was spread evenly, which was a comfortable thing to believe. This one said it was concentrated, and she knew what concentration meant when she looked at the housing data and saw the rents.

Mr. Bekele glanced in the mirror. "Fixed it?"

"Mostly," Jade said. "The map's fixed. Now I have to decide whether to present it with the demographics or without. With, and everyone sees exactly who's in that band. Without, and it's just geometry." She scrolled slowly along the river. "The person who wrote the conference guidelines said maps should be objective."

"Maps are always made by somebody," Jay said, and for once he didn't sound like he was showing off.

Jade saved the file twice, under two different names. Outside, a sign for the conference city flickered past, and the river itself appeared for a moment in the median below the highway, low and brown and patient, running parallel to them all the way in. She closed the second file, then opened it again. "Ask the first question loudly," she said to the windshield. "I'll answer that one first."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
The community hall smelled of cabbage rolls and melted butter, and Sienna stood in the doorway with her coat still buttoned, looking for a way to be somewhere else. Across town, Kobe was running sound check for his band's first paid gig, and he had asked her twice to come, and twice she had said maybe, which they both knew meant no. Her grandmother had already claimed a table near the stage, saving three seats with a scarf and a pair of mittens, and when she spotted Sienna she waved with her whole arm, unembarrassed, the way she did everything.

"You came," her grandmother said, and patted the chair. Around them, old men argued gently about a chessboard, and someone was carrying in a tray of honey cake that left a warm, spiced trail in the air. A paper icon stood on a folding table at the front, flanked by two candles that guttered whenever the door opened. January seventh, and outside, one neighbor's plastic reindeer still stood in the snow, which Sienna had always assumed was laziness.

Her mother appeared with tea, then disappeared again into the kitchen, and Sienna was handed a stack of her grandmother's recipe cards and asked to transcribe them onto fresh paper because the ink had gone brown and soft, the oldest ones nearly illegible. She bent over the table and copied out "syrniki, fry until the edges weep," and "kutya, the wheat must soak overnight," letter by careful letter, while the hall filled and the choir began a low, droning hymn that vibrated in the tabletop.

She texted Kobe under the table. I'm at my grandma's thing. He replied with a single question mark, then, what thing? It's not even Christmas anymore. Sienna stopped, her pen resting on the card. She had thought the same thing for years, that her grandmother simply celebrated late, out of stubbornness or habit, a woman who couldn't let a date go. She looked up at the icon, the candles, the small crowd of people who had all chosen this night, and typed, actually it IS Christmas for them. A bunch of Orthodox churches including the Russian one keep December 25 on the old Julian calendar, so for them it lands on January 7.

The reply took a while. so the neighbors' lights were early? she read, twice, then a third time. Her grandmother leaned over. "Who is Kobe?"

"A friend from school. He has a show tonight." Sienna hesitated. "I told him this was Christmas for you."

"It is Christmas," her grandmother said, and offered her a piece of honey cake as if that settled the matter. In a way it did. The cake was dense and sweet and faintly floral, and Sienna ate it slowly, still holding the phone, still holding the other night, the one with the amps and the smoke and the borrowed car, and she could not make both nights fit in her hands at once.

Her mother returned, read her face, and granted clemency with a glance at the clock. "The second set starts at ten. Be back by midnight or text your grandmother, not me." It was generous, and Sienna felt the cost of it immediately, because she had to leave before the carols, before the candle part, before the moment her grandmother had been describing to her since she was six. She copied one more card, the kutya one, and left it half finished, promising to finish the rest tomorrow.

The twist was waiting outside, in the parking lot, leaning against a snowbank with his hands in his pockets. "The gig fell through," Kobe said. "Bassist got food poisoning, venue double-booked, take your pick. I walked here." He looked at the lit windows, the silhouettes of singers, the plastic reindeer across the street glowing a faint, patient blue that now seemed less malevolent than simply out of sync, like a clock running in another time. "So can I come in? I want to hear the Christmas that's still happening."

Sienna looked at him, at the door, at the unfinished card on the table inside. "You have to sing," she said, and pushed the door open, and the cold let them go.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The movers had left the boxes stacked like city blocks down the hallway, and Kaitlyn carried her desk lamp out to the front step because it was the only place left to sit. The street was called Fenwick Lane, and every house on it had the same beige siding and the same young maple tied to the same wooden stake, as though the trees had been issued rather than planted. Across the road a man was winding a hose onto a reel, and when he saw her he raised a hand and called, "You must be the new family. I'm Mr. Rahimi. Number eleven." She said her name back to him and he repeated it, getting it right, which felt like more than most people managed.

Three weeks later she had been at the school long enough to learn where the good water fountain was and which stairwell smelled like wet coats, and she still ate lunch at the end of a table near the recycling bins. There were people she talked to. Norman, who sat in front of her in chemistry and drew the polymer chains in his notes with little crowns on the repeating units, had explained monomers to her once by tearing a napkin into identical squares and lining them up, and she had understood it better than the textbook. He was funny and he lent her a pencil every single day. But at 2:40 when the bell rang he said "see you" and walked off with three boys she couldn't name, and she walked to her locker feeling like a napkin square, one unit in a chain that didn't include her.

That night she called Jessy, who was still back in the old town, still at the old lunch table, and Jessy talked for eleven minutes about a girl named Priya and something hilarious that had happened in the gym. Kaitlyn laughed in the right places. When Jessy finally said, "So how is it there, do you have friends yet," Kaitlyn said, "It's fine, there are people I like," and heard how the sentence bent under the weight of what it left out. After they hung up she lay on the unfamiliar carpet and did what she always did with things she couldn't stop turning over: she looked it up.

The search took her three tries. How long does it take to make a friend, then new school no friends yet, then something about being lonely that she typed fast so it wouldn't feel like a confession. The answer that came back surprised her enough that she sat up. A 2018 study by a communication researcher named Jeffrey Hall had estimated that it takes roughly fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Fifty hours. She did the math on the back of a permission slip. Lunch was thirty minutes. Chemistry was fifty-five. If she counted only the time she and Norman actually spent talking, not just sitting in the same room, she was maybe at four hours. Maybe five.

At first the number felt like a wall. Then, walking to school the next morning past Mr. Rahimi winding his hose again in what seemed like a permanent occupation, it started to feel like something else. Not a wall, a schedule. She had been treating friendship as a thing that either happened or didn't, like weather, something you waited for and blamed yourself for when it didn't arrive. But if Hall was right, then nothing was wrong with her, and nothing was wrong with Norman, and nothing was wrong with Fenwick Lane. There was just a quantity of hours not yet spent.

She could not exactly announce this to Norman. What she could do was stay after chemistry on Thursday, because he was the only one who hadn't finished the lab and the teacher let them work while she graded at her desk. Kaitlyn pretended her own conclusion needed checking, which took ten minutes, and then they argued about whether the lab procedure was badly written, which took twenty, and Norman did his drawing of a crowned monomer on her paper to illustrate some point about repeating units and she kept it. She was ebullient all the way home, almost skipping, and she hated that she could be this happy about forty minutes, and was happy anyway.

Mr. Rahimi was out with the hose, of course. "You look pleased with yourself," he said, and she stopped, because he was the only adult on the street who had spoken to her more than once and because stopping was easier than explaining to her mother why she was grinning. She told him about the study, the fifty hours, and he nodded slowly. "So you are saying friendship is not a feeling," he said. "It is an appointment you keep." She hadn't thought of it that way, and she pushed back, because it sounded like he was reducing something to nothing, like saying love was just a monomer you repeated until you called it a polymer. He laughed and said she argued like his daughter, and she went inside feeling the conversation as another half hour banked, though she knew that wasn't how it worked with adults.

Here was the part she couldn't resolve, and she turned it over for days. The hours explained why nobody felt like a friend yet, but they didn't explain Jessy. She and Jessy had years of hours, hundreds of them, whole summers, and still the phone calls had begun to feel like visiting a museum of her own life, walking past exhibits labeled Priya and gym and Saturday. Maybe hours built a friendship but couldn't be relied on to maintain one. Maybe some part of it was a choice you kept making, and Jessy was choosing Priya, and the honest thing was to stop pretending the calls were the same as before. Or maybe, Kaitlyn thought, writing neither of these in the notebook where she was keeping her tally of hours, both things were true at once, and she would have to live in between them for a while without a study to tell her how long that took.

On Friday Norman asked, without looking up from his lab sheet, "You doing anything this weekend," and she said, "Moving more boxes, probably," and he said, "I could help. My dad has a hand truck," and she said yes before the sentence was even finished, and in her notebook that night she wrote the word Saturday and, next to it, a small crowned square.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, the narrator Nick Carraway says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.'
story:
The bus smelled of diesel and wet raincoats, and Katherine had the book open on her knees before the doors hissed shut. The Great Gatsby, paperback, cover curled at the corner where she'd bent it back on page thirty-one. She was reading the sentence for the fourth time: "I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known." Nick Carraway said it about himself, and something about it snagged in her mind like a zipper catching cloth.

"You're doing the essay for Sánchez, aren't you," Edgar said, dropping into the seat across the aisle. He had the sullen look of someone whose cross-country practice had been cancelled and who now had an unexpected hour he didn't want.

"Unreliable narrator," Katherine said. "That's the whole assignment. How the point of view shapes what we trust." She turned the book toward him. "He says this. Right there. And I can't decide if I believe him."

Justus leaned over the back of Edgar's seat, earbuds dangling. "Mr. Sánchez gave my sister that book three years ago. She said the whole thing is Nick pretending he's better than everyone he hangs out with."

The bus jolted over the railway tracks, and Katherine marked the page with her finger. "But he's the only one telling us the story. If he's lying, how would we even know?" She had a list started in the margin of her notebook, and she added to it now in pencil: hides things from us? At the party, she remembered, Nick said he'd been drunk only twice in his life, and then he got drunk that night and didn't seem to count it. And he claimed to reserve all judgements while judging practically everybody in the first chapter.

Justus was flipping through his memory of the book, or maybe his sister's summary of it. "Doesn't he say he's honest right after he's been keeping secrets for Gatsby? Like the thing with Daisy." Edgar said something about how everyone lies for their friends, and Katherine wrote that down too, because it was true and it complicated what she was building. The claim to honesty, she was starting to see, wasn't just a fact about Nick. It was a performance, aimed at the reader. You trust a narrator who announces he's honest, at least at first. That was the mechanism, if she could find a way to codify it without making her essay sound like a lab report.

"The book came out in 1925," she said. "So Fitzgerald is making this choice before anyone's arguing about unreliable narrators in classrooms. Nick says the line, and we're supposed to feel it, and then feel it curdle." She liked the word curdle. It had a certain gravitas, the kind that made teachers put check marks in margins. But she also suspected that liking a word wasn't the same as being right about it.

The bus stopped at the corner by the hardware store and three freshmen poured on, loud, shaking water off their hoods. Katherine lowered her voice. "Here's what I can't settle. Maybe Nick half believes it. Maybe everyone who says they're honest half believes it, and the lie isn't the statement, it's the certainty." She looked at Edgar, who was watching rain slide down the window in long threads. "You'd still trust him to drive you home."

"I'd trust him to drive me anywhere," Edgar said. "I just wouldn't trust him to tell me what happened after."

She laughed, then stopped laughing, because Edgar had accidentally given her the shape of the whole essay: trust isn't one thing. The reader trusts Nick's eyes and doubts his verdicts, and Fitzgerald builds the story in the gap between those two kinds of trust. She wrote gap and underlined it twice, and the bus took the long curve toward school, past the flooded field where the cross-country team usually ran.

What she couldn't resolve, and wrote in smaller letters at the bottom of the page, was whether the ending made her forgive Nick or simply recognize him. She sat with that all the way to the parking lot, book closed, thumb holding her place. When the doors opened, Justus pulled out one earbud and said, "So is he honest or not?" Katherine stood, gathered her things, and said, "Ask me in two thousand words."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Raising interest rates tends to strengthen a country's currency by attracting foreign savings, which makes imports cheaper and puts downward pressure on prices.
story:
Ava clocked in at four, tied her apron, and found Karim already stacking the olive-oil loaves with the grim concentration of someone whose mind was elsewhere. The bakery smelled of burnt sugar and flour dust, and the till drawer stuck unless you lifted it slightly, which Ms. Grant had never bothered to fix in the eleven years the place had existed.

"You look like you failed something," Ava said.

"Exchange rate." He slid the tray into the case. "Trip's in March. Rome. I've been checking the rate every night and it kept getting worse, and then last week it just turned around. My dad says don't ask why, just be grateful. But that's not an answer, that's a shrug with money attached."

Ava had been watching the same rate, for the same trip, from the other side of the same planning spreadsheet. Her savings were two hundred and forty dollars, earned mostly at this counter, and every point the rate moved was the difference between a hostel and a floor. She wanted to know why it turned around, the way she wanted to know the till trick: not because the knowing paid, but because not knowing made her feel like a mark.

That evening, on her break, she sat on the milk crate behind the flour shelves and searched on her phone with sugar on her fingertips. The central bank had raised interest rates the week before the rate turned. She read it twice, then read it aloud, quietly, to fix it in place. "Raising interest rates tends to strengthen a country's currency by attracting foreign savings, which makes imports cheaper and puts downward pressure on prices." She copied it into her notes app under TRIP, and under that she wrote: so my trip got cheaper because of something aimed at prices. She didn't fully believe the sentence yet. It felt like a spell she'd found in someone else's language.

The next shift, Chloe came in for the epicurean rye her mother ordered every Friday, and stayed leaning on the case while Ava bagged it. "Did you see the rate?" Chloe said. "My aunt thinks the bank did it on purpose. Karim says his dad thinks the bank is full of it."

"That's the thing," Ava said. "Both can be true." She laid the loaf down carefully. "The raise pulls in foreign savings, the currency gets stronger, imports get cheaper, prices come down. That's one road. But Karim's dad has a business loan, and his cousin's bakery in the next town just closed, and higher rates land on people like that first. Same decision, different doors."

"So which is right?"

"Both roads are real. I keep trying to pick a side and I can't, honestly. I know the trip got cheaper. I know something got more expensive somewhere else." She rang up the loaf. "I can hold both. That's all I've got."

Chloe paid and left, and Ava felt briefly like she'd passed a test nobody was administering. But the twist came on Thursday. Ms. Grant called her to the office behind the ovens, a room with the lineage of every recipe pinned to the corkboard in her grandmother's handwriting, and told her, apologetically, that February hours would be cut. The renovation loan had repriced. Ava did the arithmetic instantly and without mercy: fewer hours meant the improved exchange rate was saving her nothing. The same force that had opened one door had quietly closed another, and she was standing in the gap between them.

She told Karim at closing, sweeping crumbs into the dustpan while he counted the drawer with its little upward lift.

"So the rate helping my trip is the same thing cutting your hours," he said.

"Yeah. I checked it twice. I wanted it to not be true."

He snapped the drawer shut. "At least now we know what to be angry at. That's not nothing."

"It's something," Ava said. She propped the broom against the case, and outside the window the streetlights came on all at once, the way they did in winter, and she stood a moment with her hand still on the handle before untying her apron.
